title: Detector-Frame Quantum Limits For Heterodyne Timing In Relativistic Optical Links
authors: Salman Sajad Wani, Aatif Kaisar Khan, Saif Al-Kuwari, Mir Faizal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-baseline optical links for space interferometry and satellite quantum networks rely on heterodyne phase tracking under Doppler motion and gravitational frequency shifts. These relativistic shifts can generate large detector-frame beat-frequency offsets over finite readout windows and thereby constrain the temporal precision of front-end phase readout. We develop a detector-frame framework for this problem using an effective two-mode signal--local-oscillator model in which relativistic motion rescales the local-oscillator frequency. Within this setting we derive closed-form Mandelstam--Tamm and Margolus--Levitin bounds for representative Gaussian resources and connect global state distinguishability with the operational precision of heterodyne phase tracking. In the bright-local-oscillator regime we identify a geometric--operational mismatch: the joint optical state can evolve on arbitrarily short global timescales while the relevant information rate is set by the measured detector record. Combining this result with an open-loop transient-acquisition analysis, we show that white phase noise and relativistic beat-frequency drift that is approximately constant over the acquisition window generate a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal pre-lock open-loop integration window and the minimum residual phase error. These results establish detector-frame benchmarks for quantum-limited heterodyne timing in relativistic optical links and clarify how global dynamical bounds enter task-restricted continuous optical measurements.
tldr: This paper develops detector-frame quantum speed-limit bounds for heterodyne phase tracking in relativistic optical links, revealing a geometric–operational mismatch and cube-root scaling for optimal open-loop integration.
motivation: Relativistic Doppler and gravitational shifts in long-baseline optical links for space interferometry and satellite quantum networks create detector-frame beat-frequency offsets that constrain heterodyne timing precision.
method: Using an effective two-mode signal–local-oscillator model with a rescaled LO frequency, the authors derive closed-form Mandelstam–Tamm and Margolus–Levitin bounds for Gaussian resources and combine them with an open-loop transient-acquisition analysis.
result: They find that the joint optical state can evolve on arbitrarily short global timescales while the operational information rate is set by the detector record, leading to a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal pre-lock integration window and minimum residual phase error under white phase noise and constant beat-frequency drift.
conclusion: The work establishes detector-frame benchmarks for quantum-limited heterodyne timing in relativistic optical links and clarifies how global dynamical bounds enter task-restricted continuous optical measurements.

title: The Ghz Game In Black And White
authors: Terry Rudolph, Tony Newton, Dan-Adrian German
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that it is possible for three people to win the GHZ game with just the standard real valued misty state formalism, but each party will need to have two balls instead of one. That is, there will be six balls involved, rather than three. In fact, as a general rule, instead of using complex numbers in a quantum computer you can always add a qubit to "tag" complex numbers. But for proofs of non-locality, like the GHZ game, we cannot have a single universal tagging qubit, because all three parties would need access to it and therefore they could potentially transfer information via it. That's where we need to replace the one ball with three that each only need to be accessed locally.
tldr: The paper shows that the GHZ game can be won using a real-valued misty state formalism if each party uses two balls instead of one, highlighting the role of complex numbers and local tagging qubits in nonlocality proofs.
motivation: To investigate whether complex numbers are necessary for quantum nonlocality and how real-valued formalisms can simulate complex amplitudes without violating no-signaling.
method: They adapt the misty state formalism to a real-valued setting, introducing additional locally accessible balls to tag complex phases, and analyze the GHZ game under these constraints.
result: Three parties can win the GHZ game with six balls (two per party) in a real-valued misty state formalism, but a single universal tagging qubit cannot be shared because it would allow information transfer, necessitating local tags.
conclusion: While complex numbers can be simulated by adding qubits, nonlocality proofs require the tagging to be local, offering insight into resource requirements for real-valued quantum mechanics.

title: Avoiding Defects Within Heavy-Hexagon Architecture
authors: Younghun Kwon Hansol Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When implementing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing using superconducting quantum processors, one of the critical challenges to overcome is the presence of defective qubits arising from fabrication and calibration imperfections. A defect on a specific qubit severely restricts the connectivity between adjacent qubits, disrupts stabilizer measurements, induces frequent detection events, and consequently inflates the logical error rate. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been proposed, such as syndrome extraction circuits based on stabilizer folding and the construction of super-stabilizers via gauge operators. However, these methods have primarily been developed for architectures with relatively high connectivity of 3 to 4. Furthermore, experimental demonstrations showing an actual reduction in logical error rates in the presence of physical hardware defects have been lacking. In this work, we propose a defect-avoidance scheme tailored for the heavy-hexagon architecture, which features a lower connectivity of 2 to 3. While previous approaches required four measurement cycles to measure all gauge operators comprising a super-stabilizer, our proposed scheme completes all gauge measurements within only two cycles. We experimentally validate this approach on IBM quantum hardware by identifying physical defects and implementing the defect-avoidance circuits. As a result, avoiding the defect yields an approximately 10\% reduction in the logical error rate per cycle for both logical [MATH] and [MATH] errors. These findings demonstrate that defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and that defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum hardware.
tldr: A defect-avoidance scheme for heavy-hexagon superconducting architectures that completes gauge measurements in two cycles and experimentally reduces logical error rates by about 10% per cycle.
motivation: Defective qubits in superconducting processors degrade connectivity, disrupt stabilizer measurements, and inflate logical error rates, but existing defect-avoidance methods target higher-connectivity architectures and lack experimental validation on heavy-hexagon lattices.
method: The authors propose a defect-avoidance circuit tailored to the heavy-hexagon connectivity (degree 2-3), using super-stabilizers and gauge operators and completing all gauge measurements within two cycles instead of four, then implement it on IBM quantum hardware by identifying physical defects.
result: Experimental runs on IBM hardware show an approximately 10% reduction in logical error rate per cycle for both logical X and Z errors when the defect is avoided.
conclusion: Defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum devices.

title: Below-threshold Execution Of Fault-tolerant Ripple-carry Addition On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Jacob S. Nelson, Andrew J. Landahl, Andrew D. Baczewski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We deploy a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architecture based on error-detecting [MATH] and [MATH] codes on Quantinuum's Helios-1 trapped-ion quantum computer. We compile and execute ripple-carry adder (RCA) circuits for classical inputs up to five bits on this architecture. Uncomputing a workspace qubit provides an additional ``algorithmic check'' to detect errors. While available at both the physical and logical levels, this check synergizes with our architecture by increasing the effective fault distance of many circuit locations from two to four. Combining this algorithmic check with the error-detecting codes, we observed only a single logical failure in one-bit addition after burst-error filtering, yielding an estimated logical failure rate of [MATH]. This is well below the [MATH] failure probability observed for one-bit addition on the same hardware in unencoded form. Two- and three-bit adders also showed performance improvements, while the longer four- and five-bit adders executed just above threshold.
tldr: Executes fault-tolerant ripple-carry adders on a trapped-ion quantum computer using error-detecting codes and an algorithmic check, achieving below-threshold logical failure rates for small adders.
motivation: To demonstrate practical fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic on real hardware and validate an error-detecting architecture below threshold.
method: Compiles and runs ripple-carry adder circuits up to five bits on Quantinuum's Helios-1 trapped-ion quantum computer using error-detecting codes; uncomputing a workspace qubit provides an algorithmic check that increases the effective fault distance of many circuit locations.
result: One-bit addition showed a single logical failure after burst-error filtering, with an estimated logical failure rate well below the unencoded failure probability; two- and three-bit adders also improved, while four- and five-bit adders executed just above threshold.
conclusion: The work demonstrates below-threshold fault-tolerant quantum addition for small instances on trapped ions, but longer adders require further error suppression or architectural improvements.

title: Quantum-Fisher-information-aware Optimization Yields A Quantum Reservoir Advantage Over Tuned Classical Reservoirs
authors: Daniel Soh Phi Hung Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a quantum reservoir computer optimized with its quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a quantum advantage over a classical reservoir of equal readout cost, provided by a quantum-information advantage: optimizing the quantum parameters with the QFI metric. On Mackey-Glass forecasting, a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir with one to three atoms beats a tuned echo-state network at every size from 4 to 30 trained weights, by 25-69% in held-out error, and is ahead of 99.5% of 10,000 random networks. After grid and Bayesian searches saturate, the QFI-aware stage lowers the error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights, beyond equal-budget black-box search or classical-parameter gradients alone, and at 30 weights turns a loss into a win. We then derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss and factorize the gap to this bound into five link efficiencies that identify the physical mechanism limiting optimization.
tldr: A quantum reservoir computer optimized with quantum Fisher information (QFI) outperforms tuned classical echo-state networks on Mackey-Glass forecasting, with a derived QFI bound identifying the physical limits of optimization.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing promises advantages over classical approaches, but realizing them requires effective optimization of quantum parameters, which is challenging due to non-convex landscapes and limited training data.
method: The authors optimize a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir using a QFI-aware stage after grid and Bayesian searches, compare its held-out error to tuned echo-state networks of equal readout cost, and derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss, factorizing the gap into five link efficiencies.
result: The QFI-optimized quantum reservoir beats tuned classical reservoirs by 25-69% at 4-30 trained weights and surpasses 99.5% of 10,000 random networks; the QFI-aware stage further reduces error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights, turning a loss into a win at 30 weights.
conclusion: QFI-aware optimization provides a genuine quantum advantage in reservoir computing and the derived QFI bound reveals the physical mechanisms limiting optimization, offering a systematic route to improve quantum machine learning protocols.

They test their approach on the Mackey-Glass time-series forecasting task using a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir with one to three atoms. The QRC is compared against a tuned echo-state network (ESN) across a range of trainable readout weights from 4 to 30. motivation: To determine whether exact permutation covariance can supply sparse metric geometry and to expose clock and locality resource tradeoffs in finite relational quantum history Hamiltonians.
method: Analyzes norm scaling of permutation-covariant full-support k-body interaction orbits, ground-state multiplicity for graph-basis Hamiltonians, trace-distance asymmetry bounds, and constructs/solves two finite relational history Hamiltonian architectures: a cyclic clock with reversible incidence update and an order-free pair-clock architecture.

title: Exploring Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions Via The Dynamical Phase Accumulated At An Equilibrium Critical Point
authors: Han-Chuan Kou, Peng Li, Zhi-Han Zhang, Zhen-Yu Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) generated by a two-step linear quench with a finite waiting time at the equilibrium critical point. The waiting stage leads to the accumulation of a dynamical phase that depends on the waiting time and directly reflects the critical spectral structure. In the transverse Ising chain, this accumulated phase modifies the critical structure of DQPTs from a single-critical-mode (SCM) regime to a multiple-critical-mode (MCM) regime. We analytically and numerically determine the boundary between the two regimes. Along this boundary, the waiting time approaches a constant in the sudden-quench limit, whereas in the slow-quench limit it follows Kibble--Zurek (KZ) scaling with the quench time. In the SCM regime, the rate function exhibits a conventional linear singularity, [MATH], with the critical exponent [MATH] near the critical time. At the SCM--MCM boundary, this exponent changes to [MATH], leading to a divergent first derivative of the rate function. Additional discrete parameter lines with [MATH] also appear within the MCM regime in the parameter plane spanned by the waiting and quench times. Our findings establish a direct connection between the accumulated dynamical phase and the critical structure of DQPTs, further supported by an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) model.
tldr: The paper studies dynamical quantum phase transitions in a transverse Ising chain driven by a two-step quench with a waiting period at the equilibrium critical point, revealing how the accumulated dynamical phase alters the critical mode structure and scaling behavior.
motivation: Dynamical quantum phase transitions are a fundamental non-equilibrium phenomenon, and understanding how waiting at an equilibrium critical point affects them may reveal connections between equilibrium criticality and non-equilibrium dynamics.
method: A two-step linear quench protocol is used on the transverse Ising chain, with a finite waiting time at the critical point; the resulting Loschmidt amplitude and rate function are analyzed analytically and numerically, and the findings are supported by an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model.
result: The accumulated dynamical phase drives a transition from a single-critical-mode to a multiple-critical-mode regime, with the boundary determined analytically; along this boundary the waiting time follows Kibble-Zurek scaling in the slow-quench limit, and the critical exponent of the rate function changes, leading to a divergent first derivative.
conclusion: The accumulated dynamical phase directly reflects the critical spectral structure and governs the critical properties of DQPTs, establishing a connection between equilibrium criticality and non-equilibrium phase transitions that is confirmed in the SSH model.

title: Symmetric Cryptography Via Dirichlet Convolution
authors: Artur Sowa, Elias Hassani Sangani, Francis Bui, Grant Harris, Jonathan Norton
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss a new symmetric-key cipher for digital data encryption. Its implementation is fast, memory efficient, and resilient against classical, AI-assisted, and quantum attacks. Let [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] be elements of a finite abelian group [MATH] with operation [MATH] and neutral element [MATH]. Suppose one is given ciphertext [MATH]. Retrieving the plaintext [MATH] from the ciphertext is trivial when the key [MATH] is known. Without the key, however, recovering [MATH] amounts to a blind search. Even if an efficient criterion were available for identifying the plaintext among all group elements, the average number of trials would remain prohibitively large when the group is sufficiently large. The challenge in constructing a practical cryptosystem is therefore to identify a sufficiently rich group [MATH], together with efficient algorithms that enable an immersion of into [MATH] and efficient evaluation of the group operations. The proposed cipher is based on generalized Dirichlet convolution over finite fields. We investigate its security against plaintext attacks from an information-theoretic perspective. The nonlocal structure of Dirichlet convolution naturally permits plaintext salting, providing protection against plaintext attacks while allowing controlled key reuse. We establish perfect masking properties over finite fields and prove that the resulting cipher achieves information-theoretic security under key reuse when the underlying arithmetic is carried out in [MATH] with [MATH]. For arithmetic over [MATH], some information leakage remains, leading to a finite key-reuse budget.
tldr: The paper introduces a symmetric-key cipher based on generalized Dirichlet convolution over finite fields, claiming information-theoretic security under key reuse for certain field sizes.
motivation: There is a need for fast, memory-efficient symmetric encryption that resists classical, AI-assisted, and quantum attacks.
method: The cipher leverages Dirichlet convolution over finite abelian groups and analyzes its security from an information-theoretic perspective, including perfect masking properties.
result: Perfect masking and information-theoretic security under key reuse are proven for arithmetic in GF(q) with q sufficiently large, while GF(2^n) exhibits some leakage and a finite key-reuse budget.
conclusion: The proposed cipher offers a practical symmetric encryption scheme with controlled key reuse, but its contributions are classical cryptography rather than quantum information theory.

title: Can The Quantum Fisher Effective Dimension Judge A Hybrid Quantum Neural Network?
authors: Md Masum Mia, Amith Khandakar, Mohamed Arselene Ayari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pair a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is widely used to assess such models. This scalar is often interpreted as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, although these readings are rarely tested under controlled conditions. We therefore investigate what it actually measures. We define the effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, which lies between one and the parameter count, and we evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. During training, the effective dimension remains well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87, changing sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of the circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while the initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau (BP) appears at eight qubits. At a fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9, even though CIFAR-10 accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. These results show that the effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. We conclude with a practical protocol that assigns each diagnostic to the question it can answer.
tldr: The paper empirically tests whether the effective dimension of the quantum Fisher information matrix can serve as a reliable indicator of hybrid quantum neural network performance.
motivation: The quantum Fisher effective dimension is widely interpreted as a proxy for trainability or accuracy in hybrid quantum neural networks, but this interpretation lacks controlled validation.
method: The authors define effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, then evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones (including a random-projection control), four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds.
result: The effective dimension remains below the parameter count during training and correlates inconsistently with test accuracy (from -0.72 to +0.87), while backbones with the same initial effective dimension yield very different CIFAR-10 accuracies (23.14% to 86.44%).
conclusion: The effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality, and the authors propose a protocol to align each diagnostic with the question it can answer.

title: Empirical Scaling Laws Of Quantum Vision Transformers
authors: Yuqing Li, Fengyi Gao, Xin Jin, Xiaowei Jia, Qi Cheng, Junyu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is a promising application of quantum computing, yet when and how practical learning models can achieve quantum advantage remains poorly understood. Even a polynomial improvement in the resources needed to attain a given predictive performance would be significant. In this work, we investigate empirical scaling laws of quantum vision transformers (QViTs), which connect QML to the transformer architecture underlying modern large language models. We ask whether QViTs exhibit scaling behavior analogous to classical models and how this behavior changes when qubit number is included alongside dataset size and model parameters. The validation losses in our numerical image-classification experiments are well described by a joint shifted power-law model in qubit number, transformer depth, and training dataset size. Expressing this fit in terms of the classical encoder parameter budget identifies a regime in which increasing the number of qubits can compensate for fewer classical encoder parameters at comparable predicted performance. This finding is consistent with earlier observations of parameter efficiency in quantum learning models and suggests a direction for exploring possible resource savings in QML.
tldr: The paper empirically studies scaling laws of quantum vision transformers, fitting validation loss to a joint power law in qubit number, transformer depth, and dataset size.
motivation: Quantum machine learning may offer resource advantages, but the scaling behavior of quantum transformer models and trade-offs between qubits and classical parameters are poorly understood.
method: Numerical image-classification experiments with quantum vision transformers; validation losses are fitted to a shifted power-law model across qubit count, depth, and training set size.
result: The joint power law describes the data well and reveals a regime where more qubits can compensate for fewer classical encoder parameters at comparable performance.
conclusion: The findings suggest parameter efficiency in QML and motivate further exploration of resource savings, though they do not provide information-theoretic guarantees.

title: Parameter-Efficient Multilinear Readout For Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Panagiotis Markopoulos van Tien Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) uses fixed quantum dynamics as a high-dimensional feature map. Still, standard pipelines flatten reservoir measurements and train a linear readout, ignoring the natural tensor structure across time steps, qubits, and observables. We propose a multilinear readout for quantum reservoir computing (ML-QRC), a tensor-structured neural readout compressed through mode-wise projections. Relative to a dense hidden-width-64 neural readout, this reduces the feature-to-hidden parameter count from [MATH] to [MATH], giving a [MATH] feature-block compression at [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. Across Mackey-Glass forecasting and TFIM phase classification, ML-QRC remains statistically competitive with Ridge on Mackey-Glass and obtains the numerically highest full-data TFIM accuracy among tested methods, while using [MATH] fewer parameters than the full dense MLP. Its clearest benefit is improved low-data stability relative to neural MLP readouts on Mackey-Glass; this advantage does not transfer to TFIM, where Ridge performs best at 50\% data. Overall, ML-QRC is best viewed as a tensor-structured neural readout that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving QRC tensor structure, rather than as a replacement for simple linear/Ridge readouts in the tested regime.
tldr: Proposes a multilinear tensor-structured neural readout for quantum reservoir computing that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving tensor structure.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir computing pipelines flatten reservoir measurements and train a linear readout, ignoring the natural tensor structure across time steps, qubits, and observables.
method: A multilinear readout (ML-QRC) with mode-wise projections is introduced, reducing feature-to-hidden parameter count, and compared against Ridge and dense MLP readouts.
result: ML-QRC remains statistically competitive with Ridge on Mackey-Glass forecasting and achieves the highest full-data accuracy on TFIM phase classification, with improved low-data stability on Mackey-Glass but not TFIM.
conclusion: ML-QRC is best viewed as a tensor-structured neural readout that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving QRC tensor structure, rather than replacing simple linear/Ridge readouts.

title: Harmonic Reduction Of Spin-Coupled Grover Walks On Hypercubes Via Quantum Bernoulli Noises
authors: Ce Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes within the framework of quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN). We identify parity-dependent harmonic subspaces generated by the central Hamming layers: in even dimension they give a fixed-point subspace, whereas in odd dimension the walk reduces on the harmonic subspace to an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics. Using symmetric-group representation theory, we characterize the corresponding isotypic structure and determine the reduced spectrum. The harmonic reduction also yields explicit long-time probability behavior and shows that the resulting states may occupy an asymptotically vanishing fraction of the hypercube while still spanning its full Hamming diameter.
tldr: The paper analyzes spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes using quantum Bernoulli noises, identifying harmonic subspaces and reduced spectral dynamics via symmetric-group representation theory.
motivation: Quantum walks on hypercubes are useful models for quantum transport and search, but their spin-coupled dynamics and long-time behavior are complex and merit symmetry-based reduction.
method: The authors embed the walk in the quantum Bernoulli noise framework and exploit symmetric-group representation theory to characterize parity-dependent harmonic subspaces and reduced spectra.
result: They find a fixed-point subspace in even dimensions and an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics in odd dimensions, along with long-time probability behavior showing states can occupy a vanishing fraction of the hypercube while spanning its full Hamming diameter.
conclusion: The harmonic reduction provides a systematic spectral and dynamical characterization of spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes, revealing asymptotic localization-like behavior with full diameter support.

title: Compass In The Mirror: Quantum Backpropagation With The Hopf Ansatz
authors: Ranyiliu Chen Ruge Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A variational quantum state may have many control angles, and its complete gradient contains one derivative for each. The task is to turn access to selected derivatives into a shared finite-shot record for the complete vector. The Hopf ansatz supplies the setting: it constructs any normalized pure state from nested two-way magnitude splits and, for complex states, leaf phases, with one directly programmed angle per split or phase. Earlier Hopf constructions prepare the state, recover coordinates from known amplitudes, and provide indexed derivative access. With a phase-calibrated controlled reflection, the inverse Hopf frame maps each normalized magnitude direction to a computational label, so every all-[MATH] outcome contributes to every magnitude derivative. A separate signed leaf record supplies the complex phase block. A checkpoint variant reverses only the suffix below a selected depth and returns that layer's gradient block. For a complete chart with [MATH] real-valued parameters, sufficient execution counts are [MATH] for the global method and [MATH] for the complete checkpoint schedule at fixed additive coordinate accuracy and confidence. The global saving is record reuse, not a reduction of the [MATH]-entry output. Under the designated direct-angle schedules, the global method's assigned Hopf CNOT work and input/output-inclusive storage have at most logarithmic overhead relative to a matched scalar evaluation. The same Hopf geometry thus carries a state forward and the objective's complete coordinate response backward.
tldr: A variational quantum state's complete gradient can be computed via a Hopf ansatz that maps magnitude directions to computational labels, with a checkpoint variant for layer-wise gradients.
motivation: Variational quantum states have many parameters, and obtaining the full gradient efficiently is a key challenge in quantum machine learning and optimization.
method: The Hopf ansatz constructs any pure state from nested two-way splits and leaf phases; a phase-calibrated controlled reflection and inverse Hopf frame map each magnitude direction to a computational label, while a separate signed leaf record supplies phase derivatives.
result: For an M-parameter chart, the global method requires O(M) execution counts and the checkpoint schedule O(M^2) at fixed accuracy, with logarithmic overhead in CNOT work and storage compared to scalar evaluation.
conclusion: The Hopf geometry provides a unified framework for state preparation and complete gradient backpropagation, offering record reuse and efficient scaling for variational quantum algorithms.

title: Hyperpolarization-enabled Cooperative Molecular Magnetic Amplification
authors: Jingyan Xu, Raphael Kircher, Min Jiang, Xinhua Peng, Danila Barskiy, Dmitry Budker
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting weak magnetic fields at hertz frequencies is central to biomagnetism, geophysical sensing, and searches for new physics, yet it remains challenging because of technical systematics and environmental noise. Here, we realize a continuously operating molecular magnetic amplifier. Signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE) parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization maintains non-equilibrium spin order at zero field, turning scalar-coupled nuclear spins in liquid state molecules into an active, frequency-selective gain medium. Measurements of its complex magnetic susceptibility ([MATH]) reveal an intrinsic response of [MATH] 10. By feeding the collectively generated magnetic field back to the spins below the threshold for self-sustained [MATH]-oscillation, we extend the effective spin coherence and cooperatively enhance the susceptibility up to [MATH] 80. Near threshold, this produces approximately fourfold amplification of a weak (20 pT) magnetic field at 3.37 Hz at the sensor location. These results establish hyperpolarized molecules as a tunable active magnetic medium for narrowband quantum sensing and precision measurement.
tldr: A continuously operating molecular magnetic amplifier is realized using SABRE hyperpolarization and spin feedback, enabling weak magnetic field sensing at hertz frequencies.
motivation: Detecting weak magnetic fields at hertz frequencies is important for biomagnetism, geophysical sensing, and fundamental physics searches but is hindered by technical systematics and environmental noise.
method: SABRE parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization maintains non-equilibrium spin order at zero field, turning scalar-coupled nuclear spins in liquid-state molecules into a frequency-selective gain medium; magnetic field feedback below self-sustained oscillation threshold enhances the effective spin coherence and susceptibility.
result: The intrinsic complex magnetic susceptibility response is about 10, cooperatively enhanced up to about 80, yielding roughly fourfold amplification of a 20 pT magnetic field at 3.37 Hz near threshold.
conclusion: Hyperpolarized molecules can act as a tunable active magnetic medium for narrowband quantum sensing and precision measurement.

title: Sample-Size Scalability And Representation Sensitivity Of Quantum Machine Learning Models For Higgs Boson Event Classification
authors: Ankhi Roy Shiksha Bhardwaj
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum machine learning offers new approaches to multivariate event classification in high-energy physics, but its performance relative to optimized classical methods remains uncertain under limited training data and restricted quantum resources. We investigate the sample-size scalability and representation sensitivity of a quantum support vector machine and a variational quantum classifier for Higgs-boson signal--background discrimination using simulated events from the ATLAS Higgs Machine Learning Challenge. The models are trained on balanced subsets ranging from 250 to 4000 events and evaluated on held-out samples preserving the original class distribution. Principal component analysis (PCA) and autoencoder (AE) representations are examined to reduce the input dimensionality and quantum-resource requirements. Four optimized classical classifiers are used as benchmarks under a common preprocessing, validation, and evaluation protocol. We assess training-sample scalability in classical and quantum classifiers using a four-component PCA representation and examine representation sensitivity through a secondary matched-event comparison of four- and eight-component PCA representations. Within the evaluated Higgs-boson classification setting, the QSVM showed stronger performance than the VQC at larger training sample sizes, while remaining below the best-performing classical classifiers.
tldr: The paper benchmarks quantum support vector machine and variational quantum classifier against classical classifiers for Higgs boson event classification, studying sample-size scalability and representation sensitivity.
motivation: Quantum machine learning is increasingly explored for high-energy physics event classification, but its practical advantage under limited data and quantum resources remains unclear relative to optimized classical methods.
method: Using simulated ATLAS Higgs ML Challenge events, the authors train a QSVM and VQC on balanced subsets of 250 to 4000 events, with PCA and autoencoder dimensionality reduction, and compare to four optimized classical classifiers under a common protocol.
result: The QSVM outperformed the VQC at larger training sizes but remained below the best classical classifiers; representation sensitivity was assessed via matched-event comparisons of 4- and 8-component PCA representations.
conclusion: Within this Higgs-boson classification setting, quantum models show sample-size-dependent performance but do not surpass optimized classical benchmarks, highlighting the need for further advances in quantum machine learning.

title: The Weight Enumerators Of Irreducible Cyclic Codes Of Length $2^\ell$
authors: Denis E. Videla Ricardo A. Podest\'a
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using the spectral relation between irreducible cyclic codes (ICC) and generalized Paley (GP) graphs recently found by the authors, we study the weight distribution of irreducible cyclic codes of length [MATH], [MATH]. These codes were previously studied by Sharma, Bakshi and Raka, who divided them into two families (each having two cases). First we characterize the GP-graphs spectrally related to these families of ICCs: they are complete, semiprimitive, Hamming, or Cartesian products of semiprimitive GP-graphs. We then compute the spectrum of these graphs and hence, by the mentioned spectral relation we finally obtain neat explicit expressions for the weight enumerators of all the irreducible cyclic codes of length [MATH] with [MATH].
tldr: This paper derives explicit weight enumerators for irreducible cyclic codes of length 2^ℓ by characterizing and computing spectra of associated generalized Paley graphs.
motivation: Weight enumerators are fundamental invariants in classical coding theory, and earlier classifications of these codes left their explicit weight distributions unresolved.
method: The authors use a recently discovered spectral relation between irreducible cyclic codes and generalized Paley graphs, characterize the relevant graphs, and compute their spectra.
result: The associated generalized Paley graphs are shown to be complete, semiprimitive, Hamming, or Cartesian products of semiprimitive graphs, yielding neat closed-form weight enumerators for all such codes.
conclusion: The work provides explicit weight enumerators for irreducible cyclic codes of length 2^ℓ, advancing classical coding theory through spectral graph methods.

title: Ds And Amds Symbol-Pair Codes From Three Families Of Simple Root Cyclic Codes
authors: Jiawei He, Zihan Zhang, Xiaoqiang Wang, Zhao Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbol-pair distances of simple-root cyclic codes are important for evaluating error correction performance under overlapping pair read channels. In this paper, we construct three families of simple-root cyclic codes over finite fields of odd characteristic via generator polynomials. For length \(2q+2\), the minimum symbol-pair distance is \(10\) for every odd prime power \(q\ge 7\), established by excluding invalid support configurations. For length \(4q-4\), when \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) and finite field constraints hold, it is \(9\) or \(10\). For length \(2(q-1)\), reciprocal-polynomial analysis shows it is \(11\) or \(12\). All obtained codes are MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes.
tldr: Constructs three families of simple-root cyclic codes over odd-characteristic finite fields and determines their minimum symbol-pair distances, yielding MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes.
motivation: Symbol-pair distances of simple-root cyclic codes are important for evaluating error correction performance under overlapping pair read channels.
method: The authors construct cyclic codes via generator polynomials and analyze their symbol-pair distances by excluding invalid support configurations and using reciprocal-polynomial analysis.
result: For length 2q+2 the minimum symbol-pair distance is 10 for every odd prime power q≥7; for length 4q−4 under specific conditions it is 9 or 10; for length 2(q−1) it is 11 or 12.
conclusion: All obtained codes are MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes, contributing to classical coding theory for pair-read channels.

title: Quantum Annealing For Resource Allocation In Next-Generation Wireless Communication Networks: A Qubo Modeling Guide
authors: Nguyen Xuan Tung, Le Tung Giang, Mai Dinh Cong, Pham Dang Anh Duc, Nguyen Hoang Viet, Trinh van Chien, Lajos Hanzo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) offers a physics-inspired approach for such subproblems by mapping them onto an Ising Hamiltonian, which is algebraically equivalent to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model executable on quantum annealers or hybrid solvers. However, their practical employment in wireless systems critically depends on the specific problem formulation, on the particular variable encoding, constraint handling, solver selection, hardware embedding, and fair benchmarking. This paper develops wireless-oriented QUBO modeling guidelines for QA-assisted resource allocation. We first present a beginner-friendly toy example in which a terrestrial-aerial resource-allocation problem with a fractional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) maximization objective is reformulated into a two-bit QUBO via Boolean interpolation, converted into an Ising representation, and decoded back into a wireless scheduling decision. The same scheduling is applicable to UAV, aircraft, satellite, and terrestrial links in SAGIN systems. We then review the QA foundations and solver ecosystems, including binary quadratic, discrete quadratic, constrained quadratic, and hybrid models from the perspective of NG wireless optimization. Furthermore, we discuss both binary and discrete encoding, penalty-based constraint conversion, embedding overhead, solution decoding, and feasibility verification. A QUBO Compatibility Index is introduced as a lightweight diagnostic metric for assessing the associated QUBO formulation readiness, rather than a predictor of runtime or solution quality. Finally, a case study on max-min uplink power control in cell-free massive MIMO illustrates how a fairness-oriented wireless problem can be discretized, constrained, converted into the concept of a QUBO, and evaluated against classical baselines. A host of key challenges and future directions are also discussed.
tldr: This paper provides QUBO modeling guidelines for using quantum annealing to solve resource-allocation problems in next-generation wireless networks, illustrated with toy examples and a max-min power-control case study.
motivation: Resource allocation in complex wireless systems such as SAGIN and cell-free massive MIMO is computationally hard, motivating the exploration of quantum annealing and hybrid solvers as physics-inspired optimization alternatives.
method: The authors formulate wireless optimization problems (fractional SINR maximization, max-min uplink power control) as QUBO/Ising models via Boolean interpolation, binary and discrete encodings, and penalty-based constraint conversion, then benchmark against classical baselines and introduce a QUBO Compatibility Index diagnostic.
result: The toy example demonstrates a two-bit QUBO mapping back to a scheduling decision, while the cell-free massive MIMO case study shows how a fairness-oriented power-control problem can be discretized, embedded, and evaluated against classical solvers, with a diagnostic index for formulation readiness.
conclusion: The paper offers practical guidance and challenges for applying quantum annealing to wireless resource allocation, but frames itself as a modeling guide rather than a quantum information-theoretic or thermodynamic contribution.

title: Orthogonal Sc-ldpc Codes For The Ids Channel
authors: Frederik Walter, Jessica Bariffi, Antonia Wachter-Zeh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a coding scheme for the insertion, deletion and substitution (IDS) channel tailored to the short strands of DNA-based data storage. Instead of an inner synchronisation code, a spatially coupled LDPC (SC-LDPC) code is placed across the strands, with its coupling axis aligned to the position along the strands. Every decoded position thus becomes an anchor to synchronise the neighbouring strands. The decoding waves of the SC-LDPC code carry these anchors from both ends of the strands towards the middle. We bound the achievable rate from above by the information rate of a single strand and from below by that of a separated receiver. For strands of 100 nucleotides (the relevant regime for DNA-based data storage), our scheme outperforms a rate-matched concatenated construction.
tldr: The paper proposes spatially coupled LDPC codes for the insertion, deletion and substitution channel tailored to DNA-based data storage.
motivation: DNA data storage suffers from insertion, deletion, and substitution errors, requiring efficient synchronization and error correction for short strands.
method: A spatially coupled LDPC code is placed across strands with its coupling axis aligned to the position along strands, using decoding waves to propagate synchronization anchors from both ends.
result: The achievable rate is bounded by the information rate of a single strand and a separated receiver, and for 100-nucleotide strands the scheme outperforms a rate-matched concatenated construction.
conclusion: The proposed orthogonal SC-LDPC coding scheme provides an effective solution for the IDS channel in DNA data storage, improving upon existing concatenated approaches.

title: Low-Latency Ldpc Decoding Based On Consensus And Return Residual Belief Propagation
authors: Rodrigo C. de Lamare Allan E. Feitosa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose two new decoding algorithms for low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. The Consensus and Return residual belief propagation (C&R-RBP) algorithm reduces the number of iterations required to achieve a target decoding error rate over an AWGN channel by exploiting the availability of updated information, thereby mitigating the performance degradation caused by the greedy behavior of RBP-based algorithms and reducing error propagation. The Consensus and Delayed Return RBP algorithm (C&DR-RBP) achieves better performance in the early decoding iterations than C&R-RBP, making it particularly suitable for low-latency applications. Both proposed methods maintain the same computational complexity as the original RBP algorithm in terms of residual calculations. We also provide a formal analysis showing that the Consensus mechanism increases the probability of correct bit decisions under initial decoding conditions and in the presence of severe bit transmission errors, providing insight into the performance gains observed in the simulations. Numerical results based on the rapidly growing 5G New Radio (NR) standard, considering different code lengths, code rates, and channel models, demonstrate that both methods outperform competing RBP-based algorithms with similar overall computational complexity in terms of frame error rate (FER) and bit error rate (BER).
tldr: The paper introduces two residual belief propagation variants for LDPC decoding that use consensus and delayed-return mechanisms to cut iterations and latency in 5G NR settings.
motivation: Standard RBP-based LDPC decoders suffer from greedy scheduling and error propagation, which slows convergence and hurts low-latency performance.
method: The authors design C&R-RBP and C&DR-RBP, which exploit updated messages via a consensus mechanism and delayed returns while keeping the same residual-calculation complexity as RBP, and provide an analytical argument that consensus raises the probability of correct bit decisions.
result: Simulations over AWGN and 5G NR configurations with varying code lengths and rates show improved FER and BER relative to competing RBP algorithms at comparable computational cost, with C&DR-RBP excelling in early iterations.
conclusion: The proposed decoders offer a practical latency/accuracy improvement for classical LDPC coding in communication standards, but contain no quantum information component.

title: Hamiltonian-Dependent Compressibility And Physical Preservation In Approximate Quantum Compilation Using Tensor Networks
authors: Namshik Han Dohyun Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximate quantum compilation (AQC) using tensor networks provides a promising route to reducing the circuit resources required for quantum simulation. However, the factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and the extent to which compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions using AQCtensor for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a N\'eel state. By varying the exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field, we find that compression performance changes systematically with the anisotropic coupling configuration and field orientation. These variations are strongly associated with a nested-commutator measure related to second-order Trotter error, with corresponding directional trends also reflected in the target-state MPS bond dimension. For an 80-qubit quantum-hardware evaluation, AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing the total circuit depth by 45.9% and the two-qubit gate count by 47.6%. The compressed circuit exhibits comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements, while process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography provide complementary characterization beyond these observables. Together, these results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity and demonstrate substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.
tldr: The paper studies Hamiltonian-dependent compressibility in tensor-network approximate quantum compilation for an 80-qubit XYZ Heisenberg chain and demonstrates circuit reduction with high fidelity on quantum hardware.
motivation: The factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and whether compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood.
method: Using AQCtensor, the authors vary exchange anisotropy and magnetic field for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a Neel state, relating compression performance to a nested-commutator Trotter-error measure and target-state MPS bond dimension.
result: AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing total circuit depth by 45.9% and two-qubit gate count by 47.6%, with comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements.
conclusion: The results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity, demonstrating substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

title: Definition Of Multi-Parameter Super-Resolution For Optical Telescopes
authors: Peter Menart, Seungman Choi, Zubin Jacob
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Super-resolution techniques in microscopy are opening new frontiers in biology, and super-resolution for telescope imaging may provide similar benefits for astronomy and space domain awareness. Telescope super-resolution techniques such as multi-plane light conversion and photonic lanterns have been inspired by the ability of mode sorting measurements to extract classical Fisher information closer to the quantum bound than standard telescope imaging. Fisher information analyses for super-resolution imaging systems commonly consider the case of imaging point sources, but often only consider estimating a small subset of the parameters. Furthermore, there has been no demonstration of an estimation algorithm with performance that follows the limit set by the Fisher information when all point source parameters are considered. We provide a framework for defining and analyzing super-resolution using the classical and quantum Fisher information for the multi-parameter estimation problem and demonstrate an algorithm that can achieve the classical Fisher information bound for all the parameters simultaneously.
tldr: The paper defines multi-parameter super-resolution for optical telescopes using classical and quantum Fisher information and demonstrates an algorithm achieving the classical Fisher information bound for all point source parameters simultaneously.
motivation: Super-resolution techniques in microscopy inspire telescope imaging for astronomy, but existing Fisher information analyses often consider only a subset of parameters and lack algorithms achieving the multi-parameter bound.
method: They provide a framework for defining and analyzing super-resolution via classical and quantum Fisher information for multi-parameter estimation and develop an estimation algorithm.
result: The algorithm achieves the classical Fisher information bound for all parameters simultaneously, enabling multi-parameter super-resolution.
conclusion: This work extends Fisher-information-based super-resolution to the multi-parameter regime for optical telescopes, with potential benefits for astronomy and space domain awareness.

title: Entanglement-Capability-Aware Finite-Bond Circuit Cutting For Distributed Quantum Computing
authors: Weidong Liu, Qingqing Jiang, Yufu Liu, Ruiqing He, Jiandong Shang, Hengliang Guo, Qiang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum computing distributes workloads that exceed a single processor's capacity across resource-constrained components. Circuit cutting enables this decomposition, but its effectiveness depends on partition choice. We present SACE, a Simulation-Aware Circuit Partitioning framework with Entanglement-Capability-Aware Screening. EP-Cost screens partitions using a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy and native implementation cost. Under reconstruction constraints, finite-bond refinement selects the candidate that minimizes the worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at bond dimensions [MATH] and [MATH]. Across 14 exhaustively enumerated small-scale candidate spaces, EP-Cost-guided genetic algorithm selections attain co-optimal native quasiprobability decomposition (QPD) overhead, with a median within-circuit Spearman correlation of 0.9965 between EP-Cost and QPD overhead. At matched cut counts, EP-Cost reduces QPD overhead by [MATH] and [MATH] for 8- and 9-qubit QFT circuits, respectively, and improves sampled reconstruction. On 12-qubit approximate QFT, deterministic reconstruction reduces Pauli-observable mean absolute error in all six low-bond conditions and total-variation distance in five. With five cuts and 7,776 QPD terms, SACE is best on all four reconstruction metrics in four of six conditions. At 24 qubits, SACE improves exact-local QFT accuracy in all 30 instance-bond-dimension conditions against each EP-Cost-only, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baseline. The 50-qubit QFT comparisons remain favorable as reference convergence improves. Weighted QAOA circuits provide complementary, more bond-sensitive evidence. Refinement benefits persist across three search methods; larger candidate panels improve the optimized proxy without guaranteeing lower exact-local error.
tldr: SACE is a simulation-aware circuit partitioning framework that uses an entanglement-capability proxy and finite-bond refinement to improve circuit cutting for distributed quantum computing.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing must decompose large workloads across resource-constrained processors, and the effectiveness of circuit cutting depends critically on the choice of partition.
method: The framework introduces EP-Cost, a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy combined with native implementation cost, and uses finite-bond refinement to select candidates minimizing worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at two bond dimensions.
result: Across small-scale exhaustive searches and larger QFT/QAOA circuits, EP-Cost-guided selections achieve co-optimal QPD overhead with high correlation (median 0.9965), reduce overhead by up to 47% on 8-9 qubit QFT, and improve reconstruction metrics at 12-50 qubits against baselines.
conclusion: Entanglement-capability-aware screening with finite-bond refinement improves circuit cutting, though larger candidate panels do not guarantee lower exact-local error, indicating trade-offs in proxy optimization.

title: On The Fast Electrons-Optical Modes Interaction Problem Error
authors: Dmitry Churochkin Svetlana Churochkina

result: The fidelity depends on both wave vectors and their mutual orientation with the spin vector, revealing a chirality-like effect and an optimal geometric configuration.
