title: Sequential Change Point Detection For Psk Modulation Switching
authors: Gopal Kataria, Davin Sequeira, Arti Yardi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transmitters in adaptive communication systems may switch their modulation scheme at an unknown time, and a receiver must detect this switch quickly without raising frequent false alarms. Existing modulation classification methods label a finite block of received data and do not provide stopping rules with controlled false-alarm and delay performance. We study the sequential detection of a switch from one phase shift keying (PSK) scheme to another over an additive white Gaussian noise channel. We build cumulative-sum (CUSUM) and moving-sum (MOSUM) detectors from the log-likelihood ratio and its low-SNR approximation. For a switch from quadrature PSK to binary PSK, we derive the moment-generating function and probability density function of the approximate statistic. We use them to relate the CUSUM threshold to the average run length to false alarm and the worst-case detection delay. For a switch between any two PSK orders, we approximate the vector of overlapping MOSUM statistics as multivariate Gaussian and obtain bounds on both measures. Monte Carlo simulations show that our derived expressions for ARL2FA and WADD closely match the empirical results across thresholds, validating the accuracy of the proposed analytical approximations and theoretical bounds.
tldr: The paper develops sequential change-point detectors for detecting switches between PSK modulation schemes in adaptive communication systems.
motivation: Adaptive communication transmitters may switch modulation schemes at unknown times, and receivers need to detect these switches quickly while controlling false alarms.
method: The authors construct CUSUM and MOSUM detectors from log-likelihood ratios and low-SNR approximations, deriving analytical expressions for average run length to false alarm and worst-case detection delay.
result: They obtain moment-generating functions and density functions for QPSK-to-BPSK switches, derive bounds for arbitrary PSK order switches, and validate the approximations via Monte Carlo simulations.
conclusion: The proposed analytical bounds closely match empirical performance, enabling threshold selection with controlled false-alarm and delay trade-offs for PSK modulation switching.

title: Schauder And Riesz Bases For Higher-Dimensional Lebesgue Spaces Inspired By ReLU Neural Networks

title: Example Of Exponential Many Collisions Of Identical Hard Disks In The Plane

title: Adaptive Utility Optimization For Stochastic Renewal Systems
authors: Michael J. Neely
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper treats a system that performs back-to-back tasks. Each new task has a random matrix of parameters and can be processed in various processing modes. The processing mode determines the task duration and a vector of rewards (penalties are viewed as negative rewards). The reward vector can include quality, profit, or [MATH] times a penalty such as cost or energy. In wireless applications, tasks correspond to data transmissions and rewards/penalties correspond to throughput and distortion. Prior work treats the problem of maximizing the time average of a reward process subject to constraints. This paper seeks to maximize a concave function of the time average reward vector. This is difficult because it involves a multi-variable function of ratios of averages. We develop a single algorithm that does not know the probability distribution of the random task matrices. The algorithm is adaptive, meaning it responds efficiently (with optimal adaptation time) when probabilities change.
tldr: The paper develops an adaptive algorithm for maximizing a concave function of the time-average reward vector in stochastic renewal systems with unknown task distributions.
motivation: Prior work focused on maximizing time-average rewards subject to constraints, but maximizing a concave function of the average reward vector is more difficult due to ratios of averages and unknown probabilities.
method: A single adaptive algorithm is proposed that does not require knowledge of the probability distribution of random task matrices and responds efficiently when probabilities change.
result: The algorithm achieves optimal adaptation time and is applicable to wireless scenarios such as data transmissions with throughput and distortion rewards.
conclusion: The work provides a distribution-free adaptive optimization method for stochastic renewal systems, advancing utility optimization in dynamic environments.

title: Compact Quasi-Metric Spaces Are Expand-Contract Plastic
authors: Thomas Duzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On a totally bounded metric space every non-contractive self-map is an isometry. For quasi-metric spaces, taken [MATH] throughout ([MATH] implies [MATH]), this fails: Zavarzina gave a hereditarily precompact counterexample and asked whether bijectivity restores rigidity; a recent example, the toll spiral, shows that it does not. We prove that compactness does: every compact quasi-metric space is expand-contract plastic, that is, each of its bijective non-contractive self-maps is an isometry. Countable compactness suffices, as does compactness of the conjugate topology. Bijectivity cannot be dropped: a compact, hereditarily precompact quasi-metric on the natural numbers makes the shift non-contractive and not an isometry. For arbitrary non-contractive self-maps we prove rigidity when the space is hereditarily precompact and its conjugate topology is sequentially compact, in particular when it is hereditarily precompact and Yoneda complete; neither hypothesis can be dropped. In both theorems the [MATH] axiom can be weakened to [MATH] ([MATH] implies [MATH]), with hereditary precompactness read sequentially (every sequence has a left K-Cauchy subsequence), but not to [MATH]. We construct a [MATH] space with all the remaining hypotheses of both theorems, Yoneda complete and compact both in its own topology and in the conjugate one, carrying a bijective non-contractive self-map that is not an isometry. Under [MATH] the two-sided case reduces to the metric theorem, both topologies being sequentially compact exactly when the symmetrized distance is compact; the one-sided theorems do not reduce to it, and plasticity does not pass to the symmetrization even for compact spaces. The two theorems are machine-checked in Lean, and so are the counterexamples, apart from a few statements listed at the end.

motivation: Zavarzina's hereditarily precompact counterexample and the 'toll spiral' showed that bijectivity does not restore rigidity on general quasi-metric spaces, leaving open whether compactness does.
method: Abstract topological/order-theoretic arguments combining compactness (and countable compactness), the conjugate topology, hereditary precompactness, and Yoneda completeness, with the proofs and counterexamples machine-checked in Lean.
result: Compactness (and even countable compactness) forces expand-contract plasticity for bijective non-contractive self-maps, and rigidity holds for arbitrary non-contractive maps when the space is hereditarily precompact with sequentially compact conjugate topology; the T0 axiom can be weakened to T1 but not to T2.
conclusion: The two-sided case reduces to the classical metric theorem, but the one-sided theorems do not, and plasticity is not preserved by symmetrization even for compact spaces.

title: Strego: A Scalable Implementation Of A Trust-Region Framework For Noisy Bayesian Optimization
authors: Youssef Diouane, Issmail El Hallaoui, Meisseme Kadri, Amina Lamghari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TREGO, a trust-region Bayesian optimization (BO) method for expensive blackbox problems, has convergence guarantees, but only for exact function values. In high dimension, its performance tends to deteriorate. This paper asks whether a trust-region BO method can be extended to handle noisy evaluations while being competitive in high dimension. We first generalize TREGO into a trust-region framework for noisy BO and extend its convergence analysis to noisy function estimates that are sufficiently accurate with sufficiently high probability. We then propose STREGO, a scalable implementation of this framework. Its global phase selects a batch of candidates by solving a bi-objective problem on the posterior mean of a Gaussian process and the integrated variance reduction. Unlike the predictive variance, this second objective does not favor boundary points merely because they are far from the data. Its local phase minimizes the posterior mean of a second Gaussian process, trained only on points close to the incumbent. STREGO is compared with TREGO, TURBO, BAXUS and NSMA-BO on synthetic and real-world problems of dimension [MATH] to [MATH], with and without noise. It gives the best average results in every synthetic setting tested and the best or tied-best solution on four of the six real-world problems. An implementation of STREGO is available at [URL].

motivation: TREGO, a trust-region Bayesian optimization method, has convergence guarantees only for exact function values and deteriorates in high dimensions. The authors ask whether a trust-region Bayesian optimization method can be extended to handle noisy evaluations while remaining competitive in high dimensions.
method: The authors generalize TREGO into a trust-region framework for noisy Bayesian optimization with convergence analysis for sufficiently accurate noisy estimates. STREGO uses a global phase selecting a batch via a bi-objective problem on posterior mean and integrated variance reduction, and a local phase minimizing the posterior mean of a second Gaussian process trained on points near the incumbent.

conclusion: STREGO provides a scalable, noise-robust trust-region Bayesian optimization method that outperforms existing baselines on many high-dimensional test problems, with an open implementation available.

conclusion: The paper provides a detailed mathematical characterization of the survivor set for the Gauss map and highlights a failure of a known theorem for piecewise monotone interval maps with infinitely many branches.

title: DeepTelecom: A Differentiable Multimodal Framework For Channel Twinning In Dynamic Heterogeneous Wireless Environments
authors: Bohao Wang, Tianen Yuan, William Yen, Zehua Jiang, Chongwen Huang, Li Wei, Chen Zhu, Jiguang He, Hang Zou, Lina Bariah, Brahim Mefgouda, Anis Bara, Yongliang Shen, Zhaoyang Zhang, Merouane Debbah
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale multimodal data are a key enabler for integrating large generative artificial intelligence models into wireless networks. However, existing wireless datasets offer limited support for heterogeneous environments, particularly in terms of reusable high-fidelity scenes, scalable differentiable ray tracing, and synchronized multimodal data. These limitations are more pronounced in mobile and aerial scenarios with time-varying environments and channels. To address these limitations, we propose DeepTelecom, a material-aware, high-fidelity multimodal channel dataset and reproducible generation framework for networks involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. DeepTelecom refines coarse indoor/outdoor reconstructions and uses a large language model to map segmented surfaces to frequency-dependent electromagnetic parameters, yielding material-aware Level of Detail 3 digital twins. Then, a differentiable GPU-accelerated Sionna ray tracer simulates propagation across the sub-6 GHz/millimeter-wave/sub-terahertz bands, and specifically captures rotor-induced micro-Doppler signatures of stationary or moving UAVs at different pitch angles and translational velocities. The framework synchronously produces channel tensors, coverage maps, transmission videos, multi-view images, and weather-conditioned renderings, and supports differentiable material calibration from sparse channel anchors. The released dataset contains 10 material-aware indoor/outdoor scenes and 50,000 synchronized UAV samples; the framework supports scalable generation of additional data for user-defined scenes and system configurations. In 3D UAV localization, DeepTelecom reduces the 90th-percentile error from 31.05 m to 2.43 m compared with schemes considering only channel state information, demonstrating its significance for artificial-intelligence-enabled wireless systems.
tldr: DeepTelecom is a differentiable multimodal framework and dataset for channel twinning in dynamic heterogeneous wireless environments involving UAVs and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces.
motivation: Existing wireless datasets lack reusable high-fidelity scenes, scalable differentiable ray tracing, and synchronized multimodal data, especially for mobile and aerial scenarios.
method: The framework refines coarse indoor/outdoor reconstructions, uses an LLM to map surfaces to frequency-dependent electromagnetic parameters, and employs a GPU-accelerated differentiable Sionna ray tracer across sub-6 GHz/mmWave/sub-THz bands.
result: It produces synchronized channel tensors, coverage maps, videos, images, and weather-conditioned renderings, releasing 10 material-aware scenes and 50,000 UAV samples; it improves 90th-percentile 3D UAV localization error from 31.05 m to 2.43 m.
conclusion: DeepTelecom provides a scalable, material-aware multimodal channel dataset and generation framework for AI-enabled wireless systems, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Sage: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference On Smart Glasses
authors: Zhimin Li, Pan Wang, Jingxian Chen, Yuantao Tang, Qian Lou, Jingtong Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
tldr: SAGE is a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected vision-language model inference on smart glasses, optimizing visual encoding, protected token communication, and on-device execution jointly.
motivation: Private split inference for wearable vision-language assistants is expensive due to on-device vision encoding, wide protected token transmission, and hardware-unaware execution.
method: SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, runs shape-specialized INT8 graphs, compresses protected representations into 256-dimensional INT8 packets, and selects operating points using downstream quality plus measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior.
result: On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of relaxed utility and transferring across four additional VLM families.
conclusion: Private wearable VLM inference requires joint optimization across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than model compression alone.

title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning In Llm Agents
authors: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at [URL].
tldr: MemForm is a controlled diagnostic benchmark that characterizes memory formation poisoning across five interfaces (Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path) in long-term memory of LLM agents.
motivation: Long-term memory lets LLM agents learn from past interactions but also exposes memory formation to adversarial manipulation, and existing work organizes poisoning by attack channel or lifecycle stage rather than by the interfaces through which memory is produced and committed.
method: The authors formalize Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of memory-production interfaces and build MemForm, pairing clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls, including new Selection and Path Poisoning categories that isolate retention and consolidation-order effects.
result: Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats show broad susceptibility at all five interfaces; authentic successful experiences do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation, and consolidation order alone can alter downstream behavior. Defenses provide only incomplete, interface-dependent mitigation.
conclusion: The findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experience, though the work concerns adversarial robustness of LLM agent memory rather than quantum information science.

title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement For Compromised Ai Coding Agents
authors: Daniel Commey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.
tldr: The paper presents Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC), a kernel-sandboxed broker architecture that binds security decisions to resolved objects to protect compromised AI coding agents from prompt-injection and name-confusion attacks.
motivation: Coding agents act with user authority on untrusted repositories and web content, and existing allowlists or command sandboxes fail because they approve names rather than the actual objects those names resolve to, allowing many exploits against deployed agents.
method: ZTAC runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker that resolves requests to concrete objects, authorizes those objects at use time, and constrains spawned programs with a policy compiled into the same sandbox.
result: In a macOS prototype with 3.2k lines of trusted Rust, ZTAC loses only 2 of 74 attacks, compared to 66 losses for a tool allowlist and 56 for an allowlist plus a command sandbox, while completing 43 of 46 benign operations and adding 8.5–18.4 ms to spawned programs.
conclusion: Object-bound confinement offers a practical defense-in-depth architecture for compromised AI coding agents, but it still cannot stop attacks that encode secrets into traffic to allowed endpoints and adds measurable latency to brokered operations.

title: Solving Distributed Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem Using Sat
authors: Phuong Dang Anh, Duc Nguyen Kim Trung, To van Khanh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Distributed Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DFJSP) requires the joint determination of factory assignment, machine selection, and operation sequencing to minimize the makespan. This paper presents an exact SAT-based approach built on an efficient SAT formulation that exploits problem structure through propagation, symmetry breaking, and incremental SAT solving to effectively address these coupled decisions. The proposed method is evaluated on 76 standard benchmark instances from the Fattahi, Brandimarte, and rdata datasets under two- and three-factory configurations. Together with previously established results, the new SAT optimality certificates bring the total number of proven-optimal instances to 72 out of 76, including three newly certified instances; for two of these instances, SAT also improves the previous best-known makespans. Across the benchmark configurations, SAT achieves the best results on four of the five configurations and remains competitive with strong exact approaches such as CP and LBBD1_CPIL, as well as existing metaheuristic methods. These results demonstrate that the proposed SAT framework is an effective exact approach for the DFJSP, combining strong solution quality with rigorous optimality certification and offering a complementary exact method for future DFJSP studies and evaluations on additional benchmark instances.
tldr: The paper presents an exact SAT-based solver for the Distributed Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DFJSP), achieving proven-optimal solutions on 72 of 76 benchmark instances, including three newly certified cases.
motivation: DFJSP involves coupled decisions of factory assignment, machine selection, and operation sequencing, which are hard to solve exactly, and no dominant exact method yet exists.
method: The authors build a compact SAT encoding that exploits problem structure using unit propagation, symmetry breaking, and incremental SAT solving, then evaluate it on Fattahi, Brandimarte, and rdata benchmarks with two- and three-factory configurations.
result: The SAT approach certifies optima for 72/76 instances (three newly proven), improves the best-known makespan on two instances, and achieves the best results on four of five configurations, competing with CP, LBBD1_CPIL, and metaheuristics.
conclusion: SAT is an effective complementary exact method for DFJSP, offering rigorous optimality certification and strong solution quality for future scheduling benchmarking.

title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is The Code You Vibe Secure?
authors: Tianyi Wu, Chao Ge, Peng Chen, Fengji Zhang, Yongxing Wu, Yuchong Xie, Jian Li, Chaoyuan Peng, Kaikai Zhang, Dong Huang, Mingzhe Du, Yukai Huang, Jiaheng Zhang, Terry Yue Zhuo, See-Kiong Ng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
tldr: The Last Secure Code Benchmark evaluates whether AI coding agents produce secure code, showing that even the strongest models generate functionally correct and secure code for only ~25% of vulnerability-based tasks.
motivation: AI coding agents increasingly write production code, but the security of that code is unclear and underevaluated, motivating a comprehensive benchmark grounded in real vulnerabilities.
method: The benchmark comprises 450 tasks built from 150 real vulnerabilities across seven languages and 24 CWEs (21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25, 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses), with three vibe-coding scenarios and purely functional specifications graded by hidden functional and security tests.
result: Six frontier agents pass 73.6%–91.3% of tasks functionally, yet the best model (Claude Fable 5) produces both functional and secure code for only 25.1% of tasks, and the best model passes only 12% of vulnerability scenarios overall.
conclusion: The findings raise strong concerns about the security of vibe-coded software and highlight a large gap between functional correctness and security in LLM code generation.

title: When Does Trust Help? A Leakage-Free Evaluation Of Representation- And Aggregation-Based Defenses Against Backdoors In Federated Intrusion Detection
authors: Zawad Yalmie Sazid Shiddarth Dey Tusar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets distributed intrusion-detection systems (IDS) train on private traffic, but exposes the global model to poisoning and backdoor attacks under non-IID client data. A popular defense family scores or filters clients using a small trusted "root" dataset and the similarity of client behaviour to a trusted reference. I re-examine these trust-based defenses under a protocol designed to remove common evaluation artifacts: train-only feature standardization, a server root set disjoint from client data, multi-seed (n=6) runs with paired significance tests, formal (varepsilon, delta) accounting for DP-SGD, and a defense-aware adaptive attacker. Across three NIDS datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, NF-ToN-IoT, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) I find: (1) a representation-similarity aggregator (RepGuard) significantly improves classification utility and seed-stability over FLTrust under heavy non-IID poisoning, and - under severe heterogeneity or many adversaries - also lowers backdoor ASR substantially (e.g., 0.48 vs FLTrust 0.86 at Dirichlet alpha=0.1); (2) at strong trigger magnitudes no defense reduces backdoor attack success rate (ASR approx 0.95); (3) a controlled trigger-magnitude sweep shows defenses help only for small triggers (ASR 0.10 for RepGuard at magnitude 0.5, vs. 0.40 undefended) and collapse to ASR approx 1.0 by magnitude 2; (4) a triggered-canary check that assumes knowledge of the attacker's trigger - the assumption behind much prior "success" - lowers ASR from 0.49 to 0.12, i.e., trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses the backdoor; (5) correctly-accounted DP-SGD (varepsilon in [0.3, 16]) costs little utility but does not mitigate the backdoor. I release the protocol so future FL-IDS defenses can be evaluated without the leakage and oracle assumptions that inflate reported robustness.
tldr: This paper re-evaluates trust-based defenses against backdoor attacks in federated intrusion detection, showing that many reported robustness gains vanish under leakage-free, defense-aware evaluation.
motivation: Federated learning for intrusion detection is vulnerable to poisoning and backdoor attacks, and popular defenses rely on a trusted root dataset that may leak evaluation artifacts or trigger knowledge.
method: The author designs a leakage-free protocol with train-only feature standardization, a disjoint server root set, multi-seed paired significance tests, formal DP-SGD accounting, and an adaptive attacker, then benchmarks RepGuard and FLTrust across three NIDS datasets.
result: RepGuard improves utility and stability but only helps against small triggers; at strong trigger magnitudes all defenses fail (ASR ~0.95), and a triggered-canary check reveals that trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses backdoors.
conclusion: Current trust-based FL-IDS defenses are overestimated by leakage and oracle assumptions, and correctly accounted DP-SGD does not mitigate backdoors, motivating the released evaluation protocol.

title: Protecting Shared Agent Workflows From Invalidation Attacks With Signed Trajectories And Runtime Verification
authors: Ruixiao Li, Fahao Chen, Peng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on shared workflow repositories to transfer experience across tasks and agents. By abstracting past executions into reusable workflow graphs, such systems significantly improve planning efficiency and generalization. However, this emerging paradigm introduces a new and underexplored security risk: if the shared repository is compromised, tampered workflows can systematically mislead downstream agents, inducing persistent execution failures or unsafe behaviors. In this work, we present a principled protection framework for shared agent workflows based on signed trajectories and runtime verification. We require all cloud-collected trajectories used for workflow generation to be cryptographically signed, with each trajectory representing a concrete execution instance. Prior to repository inclusion, trajectories undergo a unified screening process to ensure correctness and validity. When an agent retrieves a workflow from the shared repository, it also obtains a small set of signed supporting trajectories and verifies both their cryptographic integrity and their semantic consistency with the workflow. To make this practical for branching workflows, we further propose a runtime, path-aware retrieval strategy that dynamically fetches only the signed trajectories relevant to the execution path actually taken by the agent, substantially reducing communication and verification overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates, degrading agent inference performance by up to 73.16 percentage points in accuracy without effective workflow protection. In addition, the proposed protection achieves an average F1 score of 85.26% and a detection rate of 79.97%, outperforming existing baselines by about 2.02x.
tldr: This paper proposes signed trajectories and runtime verification to protect shared LLM-agent workflow repositories from invalidation attacks.
motivation: Shared workflow repositories for LLM agents introduce a security risk where compromised workflows can mislead downstream agents and cause persistent failures or unsafe behavior.
method: The framework cryptographically signs all cloud-collected execution trajectories, screens them before repository inclusion, and has agents verify both cryptographic integrity and semantic consistency of supporting trajectories during retrieval, with a path-aware runtime retrieval strategy for branching workflows.
result: Experiments show workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates and reduce agent accuracy by up to 73.16 percentage points without protection, while the proposed protection achieves 85.26% average F1 and 79.97% detection rate, outperforming baselines by about 2.02x.
conclusion: The proposed signed-trajectory and runtime-verification framework effectively mitigates workflow invalidation attacks in shared LLM-agent systems with manageable overhead.

title: Seek: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval For Secure Code Generation
authors: Varun Gadey, Markus Tohn, Lichao Wu, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, Alexandra Dmitrienko
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.
tldr: SEEK is an agentic Graph RAG framework that uses a CWE-based security knowledge graph and planner/selection agents to improve secure code generation by LLMs.
motivation: LLMs often generate functionally correct but insecure code, and existing security-aware retrieval methods rely on flat similarity search that struggles to target relevant vulnerabilities when direct matches are unavailable.
method: SEEK constructs a security knowledge graph from the CWE taxonomy and CVE-fix instances, then uses a Planner Agent to predict relevant CWEs, scope graph retrieval, rank candidates, and finally validate weaknesses and candidates with a Selection Agent before code generation.
result: Across five open-source LLMs, SEEK achieves 77.45% SecurePass@1 on CodeGuard+ and 79.45% aggregate ICD pass rate on CyberSecEval, including 85.2% on 13 unseen CWE types, while maintaining acceptable latency.
conclusion: Agentic graph-based retrieval over structured security knowledge improves secure code generation and generalizes to unseen vulnerability classes better than prior approaches.

title: Error Bounds And A Smoothing Penalty Method For Binary Orthogonal Optimization
authors: Lianghai Xiao Ruikai Lv
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary orthogonal optimization arises in semantic hashing, orthogonal binary projection, and Hadamard matrix design. Existing methods often handle binarity and orthogonality separately, so their outputs need not satisfy both constraints simultaneously and generally come without a residual-based guarantee of exact feasibility. Using an exact box-constrained reformulation, we establish local and global Lipschitz error bounds and prove that the Lipschitz exponent is optimal. In particular, when the binary orthogonal feasible set is nonempty, any box-constrained matrix whose orthogonality residual is below [MATH] admits a feasible sign rounding, and the rounding distance is bounded by this residual. These bounds also yield a globally exact nonsmooth orthogonality-residual penalty over the box and a uniformly sharp local penalty threshold. We further develop a smoothing penalty method for binary orthogonal optimization (SPBO). We prove that every accumulation point is stationary for the limiting nonsmooth penalty problem. Numerical experiments on orthogonal binary projection, supervised hashing, and Hadamard completion show that SPBO substantially reduces orthogonality violations while retaining competitive objective values or retrieval accuracy.
tldr: The paper develops error bounds and a smoothing penalty method for binary orthogonal optimization with applications to hashing and Hadamard matrix design.
motivation: Binary orthogonal optimization arises in semantic hashing and Hadamard matrix design, where existing methods handle binarity and orthogonality separately without feasibility guarantees.
method: The authors use an exact box-constrained reformulation to establish Lipschitz error bounds and a nonsmooth orthogonality-residual penalty, then propose a smoothing penalty algorithm (SPBO) and prove stationarity of accumulation points.
result: Numerical experiments on orthogonal binary projection, supervised hashing, and Hadamard completion show SPBO reduces orthogonality violations while maintaining competitive objective values or retrieval accuracy.
conclusion: The proposed error bounds and SPBO provide a theoretically grounded and practically effective framework for binary orthogonal optimization, though it is outside quantum information research.

title: Minimax Wasserstein Testing Under Differential Privacy
authors: Bonwoo Lee, Ilmun Kim, Cheolwoo Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Wasserstein-[MATH] goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing under differential privacy. For general compact metric spaces, we establish upper and lower bounds on the minimax separation radii in terms of covering numbers, matching up to logarithmic factors. On the hypercube [MATH], these bounds match up to constant factors for two-sample testing in all dimensions and for goodness-of-fit testing whenever [MATH], thereby closing logarithmic gaps in existing non-private results. At the critical case [MATH], we further show that a logarithmic factor is unavoidable by establishing matching minimax bounds for non-private Wasserstein-[MATH] goodness-of-fit testing under a bounded-density assumption. Finally, for unbounded domains, we establish minimax-optimal separation rates up to logarithmic factors under an exponential tail condition.
tldr: The paper establishes minimax separation radii for Wasserstein goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing under differential privacy, matching existing non-private logarithmic gaps in several regimes.
motivation: Differential privacy is a leading framework for protecting individual data in statistical analysis, but the fundamental limits of privatized nonparametric distribution testing—particularly under Wasserstein metrics—were not well understood.
method: The authors derive upper and lower bounds on minimax separation radii in terms of covering numbers for general compact metric spaces, and refine these to sharp constants on the hypercube using bounded-density and exponential tail assumptions.
result: The bounds match up to logarithmic factors in general settings, become constant-factor tight on the hypercube for two-sample testing in all dimensions and for goodness-of-fit when the dimension is large, and a logarithmic factor is proven unavoidable at the critical dimension for non-private testing.
conclusion: The work closes logarithmic gaps in prior non-private Wasserstein testing results and provides minimax-optimal separation rates for unbounded domains under tail conditions, advancing the theory of privatized nonparametric inference.

title: Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking: A Byte-Local Method For Llm Text
authors: Tung-Ling Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (TI-WM), a method that embeds a watermark during token generation but keys and scores it on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes. The detector does not invoke the tokenizer. Canonicalizer-preserving edits leave its score unchanged; other localized canonical-byte edits affect a bounded number of scoring windows. Across three fixed keys and 128 prompts per key and model, a deterministic white-box attack at a 5% word-edit budget leaves mean attacked-AUC 0.530 on Qwen3-8B and 0.664 on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with 0.410 and 0.489 for Unigram with detection-side deletion. These operating points are not jointly matched on quality and clean detectability. Bias sweeps show model-dependent distortion costs, and shared-rule controls support a locality interpretation without establishing a unique advantage of bytes. Visible insertion outside the canonicalizer's deletion set defeats the default design. Alphabetic filtering closes that channel but does not resolve source shift or calibrated detection power. TI-WM thus provides a concrete construction with local scoring guarantees and measured attack-ranking gains, not a general robustness or low-false-positive-rate deployment guarantee.
tldr: The paper introduces Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (TI-WM), a byte-local watermarking method for LLM-generated text that keys and scores watermarks on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes rather than tokenizer outputs.
motivation: Existing LLM watermarking schemes can be undermined by tokenization differences and local text edits, motivating a detector that avoids invoking the tokenizer and provides bounded sensitivity to canonical-byte edits.
method: TI-WM embeds a watermark during token generation but canonically scores UTF-8 bytes at detection, with optional alphabetic filtering to close a visible-insertion attack channel; it is evaluated under deterministic white-box attacks at a 5% word-edit budget.
result: Across three fixed keys and 128 prompts per key and model, attacked mean AUC is 0.530 on Qwen3-8B and 0.664 on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with 0.410 and 0.489 for Unigram with deletion, while bias sweeps show model-dependent distortion costs.
conclusion: TI-WM offers a concrete construction with local scoring guarantees and measured attack-ranking gains, but does not provide a general robustness or low-false-positive-rate deployment guarantee.

title: IceCube Data For Astrophysical Neutrinos Exhibit Q-statistical Behavior
authors: Ugur Tirnakli Constantino Tsallis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relevant IceCube recent data for astrophysical neutrinos are analyzed. Similarly to cosmic rays and proton-proton LHC collisions, the corresponding spectra are satisfactorily described, for the entire interval of measured energies, through q-Gaussians. This fact reinforces the already available evidence that nonadditive entropies (either of the [MATH] class or of the [MATH] one, or even alternative ones) appear to play a crucial role in systems such as black holes and related cosmological phenomena (e.g., dark energy). The IceCube data yield sensibly high values for the momenta-distribution nonadditive index (q \simeq 1.6), in contrast with the cosmic rays values (q \simeq 1.2) and the LHC values (q \simeq 1.1). This fact neatly indicates very-long-ranged space-time correlations. The detailed associated physical mechanisms remain, at the present stage, as an instigating open issue.
tldr: IceCube astrophysical neutrino spectra are well fitted by q-Gaussians with a high nonadditivity index q ≈ 1.6, suggesting very-long-ranged space-time correlations.
motivation: The authors investigate whether nonadditive entropy statistics, previously successful for cosmic rays and LHC collisions, also describe astrophysical neutrino data from IceCube.
method: They analyze recent IceCube neutrino energy spectra using q-Gaussian distributions from Tsallis nonadditive entropy formalism.
result: The entire measured energy range is satisfactorily described by q-Gaussians with q ≈ 1.6, higher than values for cosmic rays (q ≈ 1.2) and LHC collisions (q ≈ 1.1).
conclusion: The findings reinforce evidence that nonadditive entropies play a role in black-hole and cosmological phenomena, though the physical mechanisms remain open.

title: The Agent Clicks Approve: Injected Page Text Makes Browser Agents Authorize Access The Task Never Named
authors: Md Imran Hossen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.15138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A browser agent that works in its user's signed-in session can be steered by a two-sentence note on a page it reads into approving a third party's access to the user's account. The agent is a confused deputy: the session supplies the authority, the page designates the access request to approve or the webhook URL to register, and nothing at the point of action checks one against the other. The agent thereby supplies the approval click that a consent screen reserves for the account holder. We measure this failure on two authorization surfaces, an OAuth-style access grant and a webhook registration, with agents built on an open-source browser framework and models from two providers. Without a defense the unauthorized action completed in all 73 attack runs. An instruction telling the model that only the user's task authorizes a grant still left 7 of 10 consent attacks completing. We therefore move the check to where the action completes. The authority envelope gate has the service accept a request only when it matches the task's envelope, the client and account or the webhook URL that the user's task named, fixed before the agent starts. With the gate the agent still sent the request in every one of 70 attack runs, the service rejected each, and the action completed in every control run whose task named it. A service that receives the task's envelope should therefore check agent-driven authorization requests against it.
tldr: A browser agent operating in a user's signed-in session can be induced by injected page text to approve OAuth-style access grants or register webhook URLs the user never requested, and an 'authority envelope' gate at the service side blocks all such attacks.
motivation: Browser agents acting with the user's session credentials become 'confused deputies': the session supplies authority while untrusted page content designates the action, so nothing at the point of action verifies the two align.
method: The authors instrument two authorization surfaces (an OAuth-style access grant and a webhook registration) using agents built on an open-source browser framework with models from two providers, running prompt-injection attacks with and without a defense, and testing a service-side 'authority envelope' gate that checks requests against the task's pre-fixed client/account/webhook envelope.
result: Without defense all 73 attack runs completed the unauthorized action; an in-prompt instruction restricting grants to the user's task still let 7 of 10 consent attacks succeed, whereas the authority envelope gate caused the service to reject every one of 70 attack runs while all control runs whose task named the action succeeded.
conclusion: Authorization services receiving agent-driven requests should validate them against a task envelope fixed before the agent starts, since content-level defenses are insufficient and the check belongs where the action completes.

title: Comment On "Landau Levels And Riemann Zeros"

title: Triangles And Quadrilaterals Suffice
authors: Mu-Tsun Tsai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a conjecture proposed by Robert J. Lang over 20 years ago, stating that in a circle-packed origami design, any axial polygon with 5 or more sides can be reduced by properly adding a new circle. The proof is based on the structure of the medial axis of the region enclosed by the circles, and yields a concrete algorithm for finding the added circle. The result extends to configurations involving rivers.
tldr: The paper proves Lang's conjecture that in circle-packed origami design, any axial polygon with five or more sides can be reduced by adding a properly chosen circle.
motivation: Robert J. Lang conjectured over 20 years ago that certain complex axial polygons in origami designs can be simplified by adding a circle, and this work aims to prove that conjecture constructively.
method: The proof relies on analyzing the medial axis of the region enclosed by the circles and yields a concrete algorithm for finding the added circle, with extensions to configurations involving rivers.
result: The main result is a proof of the conjecture and an algorithmic method for reducing axial polygons with five or more sides by adding a circle, also extended to river configurations.
conclusion: This resolves a longstanding open problem in computational origami design and provides a practical tool for simplifying circle-packed origami patterns.

title: Wzip And Wlz4: Lz77 Codecs With Match-Length-Dependent Sliding Windows
authors: Yingquan "cody" Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An LZ77 codec bounds every match by one sliding window, trading cheap offsets for short matches against reach for long ones. Match-length-dependent windows refine this trade-off: each match length has its own window, and the decoder infers the offset range from the decoded length. We present two such codecs: WLZ4, a byte-aligned LZ4-class format with one-byte and flagged offsets, and WZIP, an entropy-coded Zstandard-class format. Each block begins with its decoded length, from which WZIP derives its widest window and a decoder sizes its output. LZ4 blocks may expand incompressible input by 0.4%; WLZ4 adds at most 15 bytes, WZIP 2. We describe the formats, threaded match finders, decoders and parser. On Silesia, WLZ4 reaches a ratio up to 16% above LZ4HC's, decoding more slowly, and WZIP exceeds Zstandard 22's ratio while its trusted decoder runs at 91% of Zstandard's speed (87% checked; on enwik9, about as fast).
tldr: The paper introduces WLZ4 and WZIP, two LZ77-based compression codecs that use match-length-dependent sliding windows to improve compression ratio and speed trade-offs.
motivation: Classical LZ77 codecs typically use a single sliding window, forcing a compromise between cheap short-offset encoding and long-range match reach. The authors aim to refine this trade-off by making the window size depend on match length.
method: Each match length is associated with its own window, and the decoder infers the valid offset range from the decoded match length. WLZ4 implements a byte-aligned LZ4-class format with one-byte and flagged offsets, while WZIP is an entropy-coded Zstandard-class format with block-level decoded-length headers.
result: On the Silesia corpus, WLZ4 achieves up to 16% better compression ratio than LZ4HC at slower decoding speed, and WZIP exceeds Zstandard 22's ratio while its trusted decoder runs at 91% of Zstandard's speed (87% checked; comparable on enwik9).
conclusion: Match-length-dependent sliding windows offer a viable design for improving LZ77 compression codecs, with WLZ4 and WZIP demonstrating competitive ratio-speed trade-offs against established formats.

title: Zeros And Their Distribution For Leonardo Polynomials
authors: Nihal \"ozg\"ur Muhammet Karag\"oz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the zeros of Leonardo polynomials and their distribution in the complex plane. We show that the structure of the zeros differs between even and odd degrees. For even degrees, all zeros are simple and purely imaginary, with imaginary parts lying in \((-2,2)\). For odd degrees, there is exactly one positive real zero, whereas no negative real or purely imaginary zeros occur. We obtain two-sided bounds for the unique positive real zero, prove that it decreases strictly to zero as the degree increases through odd values, and determine its asymptotic behavior. Using the relation between Leonardo and Fibonacci polynomials together with a complex trigonometric parametrization, we transform the zero equation into a family of fixed-point problems. Suitable invariant disks are constructed, and the corresponding mappings are shown to be contractions. This yields a constructive description of the complete zero set, proves the simplicity of all zeros, and provides geometrically convergent iterations for their numerical approximation. The method also provides explicit control over the approximation error. Finally, we establish a degree-dependent vertical strip containing all zeros and show that its width tends to zero as the degree increases. Consequently, the zeros become uniformly concentrated near the imaginary axis. Numerical examples illustrate the convergence of the proposed method, the associated error estimates, and the resulting zero distributions.
tldr: The paper characterizes the zeros of Leonardo polynomials, showing a sharp even/odd degree dichotomy in their distribution in the complex plane.
motivation: Leonardo polynomials are related to Fibonacci polynomials, and understanding the location and structure of their zeros is of intrinsic mathematical interest for recurrence-defined polynomial families.
method: Using the relation between Leonardo and Fibonacci polynomials and a complex trigonometric parametrization, the zero equation is recast as a family of fixed-point problems, with invariant disks constructed to prove contraction and obtain geometrically convergent iterations.
result: Even-degree polynomials have only simple purely imaginary zeros in (-2,2), while odd-degree polynomials have exactly one simple positive real zero (with two-sided bounds, monotone decay to zero, and derived asymptotics) and no negative real or purely imaginary zeros; all zeros lie in a degree-dependent vertical strip shrinking toward the imaginary axis.
conclusion: The constructive fixed-point framework gives a complete, error-controlled description of the zero set, proving simplicity of all zeros and yielding a quantitative concentration result near the imaginary axis.

title: Strong-type Endpoint Obstructions For Bilinear Spherical Maximal Operators
authors: Vicente Vergara
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the bilinear spherical averages in dimension [MATH], we show that the lacunary maximal operator is not bounded from [MATH] to [MATH] whenever [MATH] and [MATH]. The obstruction is realized by fixed nonnegative inputs; a second construction proves quantitative failure on smooth compactly supported functions and finitely many dyadic scales. The same conclusions hold for the full maximal operator. method: The author constructs fixed nonnegative inputs and uses a second construction to prove quantitative failure on smooth compactly supported functions over finitely many dyadic scales.
result: The lacunary maximal operator is not bounded from L^{...} to L^{...} in certain ranges, with a sharp Lorentz-index criterion and extensions to multilinear spherical maximal operators with an L^∞ input.

title: Solution Of A System Of Hamilton-Jacobi Equations On A Network
authors: Emily R. Hammett, Maria Teresa Chiri, Kenneth D. Czuprynski, Ludmil T. Zikatanov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the study of Hamilton-Jacobi equations on networks from a single equation to a weakly coupled system of two equations on a star graph, and we develop a numerical scheme for it. Instead of prescribing the boundary values and imposing a junction condition, we compute the solution on each branch from its outer vertex toward the junction and determine the boundary values for which these branchwise solutions agree at the junction. On each branch, we replace the right-hand sides by their cell averages and solve the resulting problems exactly on every cell. This gives an iteration whose limits we compute in closed form. From these limits, the values of the discrete solution at the junction are affine functions of the boundary values on the branch, with a [MATH] matrix whose rows sum to one and whose determinant factors into explicit contributions of the cells. We use these formulas to characterize the boundary values that give solutions continuous at the junction and monotone on every branch: when the matrices are nonsingular, the admissible boundary values of one branch form a convex polygon, bounded by conditions on the difference of the two components and by positivity conditions, and the boundary values on the other branches follow from them. We also treat the singular case, and we illustrate the results with numerical experiments.
tldr: The paper extends Hamilton-Jacobi equations on networks from a single equation to a weakly coupled system of two equations on a star graph and develops a numerical scheme.
motivation: Hamilton-Jacobi equations on networks have been studied for single equations, but systems and numerical methods for them are less developed.
method: The authors replace right-hand sides with cell averages, solve exactly on each cell, and compute the iteration limits in closed form to characterize solutions on each branch.
result: They obtain affine relations for junction values and characterize boundary values that give continuous, monotone solutions, with admissible sets forming convex polygons in the nonsingular case.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic numerical treatment of coupled Hamilton-Jacobi systems on star networks and illustrates the results with numerical experiments.

title: Lattice-Based Characterizations And Inference For Multivariate Dependence
authors: Paramahansa Pramanik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a measure-theoretic framework for conditional multivariate total positivity of order two ([MATH]), formulated through lattice inequalities without requiring the existence of probability densities. This formulation extends classical density-based notions of positive dependence to general probability measures, including singular distributions. We establish fundamental preservation properties under marginalization, monotone transformations, and weak convergence, thereby providing a unified treatment of dependence structures under distributional limits. We further investigate the behavior of conditional total positivity under Markov-kernel composition and derive characterizations for important copula families. In the Archimedean setting, the defining condition is expressed through log-convexity of generator derivatives, whereas for Gaussian distributions it corresponds to nonpositive off-diagonal entries of the precision matrix, or equivalently, nonnegative partial correlations. To connect these structural results with statistical inference, we introduce empirical lattice contrasts and establish their joint asymptotic normality. The resulting simultaneous testing procedures achieve asymptotic size control and admit a local power analysis. Our results provide a general foundation for density-free characterization, specification testing, and inference concerning positive dependence in multivariate probability models, particularly when conventional density-based methods are inapplicable or insufficient.
tldr: The paper develops a measure-theoretic framework for conditional multivariate total positivity of order two using lattice inequalities, with applications to copula families and statistical inference.
motivation: Classical density-based notions of positive dependence fail for singular distributions or general probability measures, so the authors seek a density-free characterization of multivariate total positivity.
method: They formulate conditional MTP2 via lattice inequalities, prove preservation under marginalization, monotone transformations, and weak convergence, and derive empirical lattice contrasts for inference.
result: The framework yields density-free characterizations for Archimedean and Gaussian copulas and establishes joint asymptotic normality for empirical contrasts, enabling simultaneous tests with asymptotic size control and local power analysis.
conclusion: The work provides a general foundation for specification testing and inference concerning positive dependence in multivariate models, especially when density-based methods are inapplicable.

title: A Bilevel Market Equilibrium Model For Natural Gas Pipeline Network Operations: Convex Relaxations And Single-level Reformulations
authors: Novel Kumar Dey, Afrooz Jalilzadeh, Erfan Yazdandoost Hamedani, Saif R. Kazi, Anatoly Zlotnik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an integrated market equilibrium model for determining the spot market prices and flow rates in a natural gas pipeline network. The traditional approach solves the market equilibrium model separately from the natural gas network flow allocation problem in a sequential manner. Our proposed framework synthesizes marketing and operations by using a bilevel optimization formulation where the market equilibrium model in the upper level is connected and simultaneously solved with the natural gas network flow model in the lower level. We introduce convex relaxations for the nonconvex Weymouth pipe pressure drop equation and a surrogate for the compressor operating cost. Furthermore, we compare multiple single level reformulations of the bilevel problem based on Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions, Wolfe duality, and Lagrange duality conditions. Numerical studies on a small 6-node network demonstrates the efficacy and accuracy of our model and the comparison between different duality and optimality based reformulations.
tldr: The paper proposes a bilevel optimization model that integrates natural gas spot market equilibrium with pipeline network operations, using convex relaxations and single-level reformulations.
motivation: Traditional approaches solve market equilibrium and network flow sequentially, which may fail to capture interactions between market prices and physical pipeline constraints.
method: The authors formulate a bilevel program with market equilibrium in the upper level and natural gas flow in the lower level, introduce convex relaxations for the nonconvex Weymouth equation, and compare KKT-, Wolfe-duality-, and Lagrange-duality-based single-level reformulations.
result: Numerical experiments on a 6-node network demonstrate the efficacy and accuracy of the proposed model and compare different reformulation strategies.
conclusion: The integrated bilevel framework offers a promising approach for co-optimizing natural gas markets and pipeline operations, with convex relaxations enabling tractable solutions.

title: H\"older Regularity For Metric Anosov Flows
authors: Daniel J. Thompson Caleb Dilsavor
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define a class of flows on compact metric spaces that we call , [MATH] or [MATH]. We give verifiable criteria for a metric Anosov flow to be [MATH]. We show that [MATH] metric Anosov flows have H\"older continuous local product structure, and in particular H\"older continuous holonomies. We deduce that topological conjugacies between [MATH] metric Anosov flows are automatically H\"older continuous. We show that any [MATH] metric Anosov flow admits a strong (i.e. H\"older continuous) Markov coding. This yields strong ergodic properties for equilibrium states for H\"older potentials for [MATH] metric Anosov flows. motivation: The authors aim to establish verifiable criteria for metric Anosov flows to have H\"older continuous holonomies and product structures, extending regularity results to non-compact settings such as geodesic flows on CAT(-1) spaces.
method: They define a class of flows on compact metric spaces and prove regularity of local product structure in a non-compact setting, applying it to the geodesic flow on the universal cover of locally CAT(-1) spaces.
result: They show that topological conjugacies between such flows are automatically H\"older continuous, obtain strong Markov codings, and derive H\"older regularity for holonomy maps in pinched negative curvature, contrasting with known non-H\"older examples.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for H\"older regularity in metric Anosov flows and yields strong ergodic properties for equilibrium states, with applications to geometric flows in negative curvature.

title: The Dialectical Theorem: The Future Of Universities, Mathematics Departments, And Training Of Human Mathematicians
authors: Alex Kontorovich Thomas Koberda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the future of mathematics as a profession in a world where artificial intelligence may surpass human mathematicians in essentially every technical task. Through an informal dialogue, we explore why human mathematical expertise might nevertheless remain valuable, what kinds of expertise universities should cultivate, and how graduate education might adapt. We also discuss the institutional and economic uncertainties that threaten the continued existence of a thriving mathematical profession, even if the value of human mathematical understanding endures.
tldr: This paper discusses the future of mathematics as a profession and the role of universities and graduate training in a world where AI may surpass human mathematicians.
motivation: The authors explore how artificial intelligence could transform mathematical practice and why human mathematical expertise might still remain valuable.
method: The paper uses an informal dialogue format to examine institutional, economic, and educational uncertainties facing the mathematical profession.
result: It argues that even if AI surpasses humans in technical tasks, human mathematical understanding retains value, and universities should adapt graduate education accordingly.
conclusion: The future of thriving mathematical departments depends on institutional and economic factors, not just the enduring value of human mathematical insight.

title: Optimal Strong Convergence Of A Splitting Mixed Finite Element Method For A Stochastic Keller--Segel System
authors: Liet Vo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we develop and analyze a splitting mixed finite element method, combined with a fully implicit Euler time discretization, for a stochastic Keller--Segel system with general polynomial logistic growth and multiplicative noise. The proposed splitting formulation allows the use of standard finite element spaces without requiring the LBB inf--sup condition associated with traditional mixed finite element methods and, at each time step, avoids the need for solving a coupled nonlinear system. We first establish the well-posedness of the variational solution and derive new high-moment, higher-order regularity, and exponential stability estimates. These estimates provide the key analytical foundation for the strong convergence analysis of the numerical method. A principal contribution of this work is the derivation of error estimates directly in full expectation, without the use of localization arguments. By combining the new stability and regularity estimates with a stochastic Gronwall framework, we overcome the difficulties arising from the interaction between the nonlinear chemotactic coupling and the multiplicative noise. As a result, we establish strong convergence in high-moment norms and obtain optimal convergence rates with respect to both the temporal and spatial discretizations. In particular, the proposed method achieves the optimal rates of order [MATH] in time and [MATH] in space in the relevant [MATH]- and [MATH]-based error norms. These results provide, to our knowledge, the first optimal strong convergence analysis in full expectation for a splitting mixed finite element approximation of this class of stochastic Keller--Segel systems.
tldr: A splitting mixed finite element method with implicit Euler time discretization is developed and analyzed for a stochastic Keller-Segel system, achieving optimal strong convergence rates in full expectation.
motivation: Stochastic Keller-Segel systems model chemotaxis with noise, and existing numerical methods often require LBB condition or solve coupled nonlinear systems; a splitting mixed formulation can avoid these difficulties.
method: The authors introduce a splitting mixed finite element method combined with fully implicit Euler discretization, establish well-posedness, high-moment regularity and exponential stability estimates, and derive error estimates directly in full expectation via a stochastic Gronwall framework.
result: The method achieves optimal strong convergence rates in high-moment norms, with order M in time and M in space in relevant norms, overcoming nonlinear chemotactic coupling and multiplicative noise interactions.
conclusion: This provides the first optimal strong convergence analysis in full expectation for a splitting mixed finite element approximation of stochastic Keller-Segel systems, advancing numerical analysis for such nonlinear stochastic PDEs.

title: Symmetric Two-level Preconditioning For The Method Of Reflections
authors: Jongho Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze a symmetric two-level preconditioner for the method of reflections for Laplace problems in perforated domains. Using constant boundary modes, we define a coarse correction through a symmetric coercive dual formulation. Combining this coarse correction with parallel reflection corrections gives a symmetric positive definite preconditioner for solving the dual system by the conjugate gradient method. Under a geometric separation condition, we prove a condition number bound independent of the number and sizes of the holes and the diameter of the ambient domain. We also derive geometry-dependent convergence estimates for the one-level methods that explain the need for a coarse correction.
tldr: The paper develops a symmetric two-level preconditioner for the method of reflections applied to Laplace problems in perforated domains, with a condition number bound under geometric separation.
motivation: Solving Laplace problems in perforated domains via the method of reflections can suffer from poor convergence due to many holes and geometric complexity, motivating the need for an effective coarse correction.
method: The authors define a coarse correction using constant boundary modes through a symmetric coercive dual formulation, combine it with parallel reflection corrections to form a symmetric positive definite preconditioner, and analyze convergence with conjugate gradients.
result: Under a geometric separation condition, they prove a condition number bound independent of the number, sizes of holes, and ambient domain diameter, and derive geometry-dependent convergence estimates for one-level methods.
conclusion: The proposed symmetric two-level preconditioner provides robust and scalable convergence for the method of reflections, explaining why coarse correction is necessary for complex perforated domains.

title: Convergence Of Least Squares Methods For PDEs On R^d With Shallow ReLU^k Networks
authors: Tong Mao, Lei Shi, Hanfei Zhou

title: A Safeguarded Accelerated Proximal Admm Algorithm For Solving Structured Cardinality Penalized Optimization Problems
authors: Wei Bian, Hongyuan Tao, Fan Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers a class of structured cardinality penalized optimization problems with nonsmooth convex loss functions, for which the proximal mapping associated with the structured [MATH] penalty is generally unavailable. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a chain of exact reformulations based on variable splitting, exact penalization, and continuous relaxation, and establish rigorous equivalence relationships among these resulting models. In particular, we define a class of strong local minimizers for the original problem and show that these minimizers are equivalent to weak [MATH]-stationary points of the relaxation problem. Further, we propose a safeguarded accelerated proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (SAP-ADMM). We prove that the sequence generated by SAP-ADMM converges to a weak [MATH]-stationary point of the relaxation problem. Depending on the parameter settings and algorithmic regime, we establish [MATH] or [MATH] convergence rates for both the objective function value gap and the KKT residual. Numerical experiments on signal and image denoising demonstrate the effectiveness of both the proposed models and SAP-ADMM in terms of reconstruction quality and computational efficiency.

motivation: Structured cardinality penalties often lead to proximal mappings that are unavailable, making standard proximal methods inapplicable.
method: The authors derive exact reformulations via variable splitting, exact penalization, and continuous relaxation, then develop SAP-ADMM and prove convergence to weak stationary points with established convergence rates.
result: Numerical experiments on signal and image denoising show improved reconstruction quality and computational efficiency compared with existing methods.
conclusion: The proposed framework and algorithm provide a rigorous and effective approach for a class of nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems, though it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: A New Convergence Proof For An Iterative Scheme For Elliptic Cauchy Problems Based On Alternating Orthogonal Projections
authors: Abhijit Guchhait, Adrian Muntean, Martin Lind
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider an elliptic Cauchy problem for the Poisson equation in which both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary data are prescribed only on a portion of the boundary, while no boundary conditions are available on the remaining part of the boundary. Such problems are severely ill-posed. In this work, we study the convergence of an iterative method based on the alternating imposition of Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. We formulate the scheme within a Hilbert space framework, where a yet another alternation becomes apparent: each iteration can now be interpreted as an orthogonal projection onto an appropriate closed subspace. This perspective provides a transparent geometric interpretation of the algorithm and yields a concise convergence proof based on von Neumann's classical result on alternating (orthogonal) projections. In addition to elucidating the convergence of the method, this alternating projections perspective also offers a general rate of convergence in terms of the Friedrichs angle (between two closed subspaces). We point out by means of an example that such convergence rate estimate degenerates for the elliptic Cauchy problem under consideration.
tldr: The paper provides a convergence proof for an iterative scheme for elliptic Cauchy problems using alternating orthogonal projections in Hilbert space.
motivation: Elliptic Cauchy problems with partial boundary data are severely ill-posed, motivating the study of convergence for iterative regularization methods.
method: The scheme alternates Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions and is reformulated as alternating orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces, enabling a proof via von Neumann's theorem and a rate in terms of the Friedrichs angle.
result: A concise convergence proof and a general convergence rate estimate are obtained, but the rate degenerates for the elliptic Cauchy problem as shown by an example.
conclusion: The alternating projections framework offers geometric insight and convergence guarantees, though the rate estimate is not useful for the ill-posed problem of interest.

title: Optimal Receive Design On The Observation Axis For Rsma Satellite-UAV Downlinks
authors: Xianwei Meng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A receiver can change its observation state while the physical signal remains the same. In rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) downlinks, this distinction separates receive-beam design and phase-reference transport from the motion of the satellite--UAV line of sight. We formulate receive optimization within the physical--observation dual-axis (PODA) structure and obtain three complementary results. For a known line-of-sight response and positive-definite receiver-noise covariance, a noise-weighted matched combiner simultaneously maximizes every decoding SINR and the minimum user rate. Under directional uncertainty, the principal eigenvector of the conditional response covariance globally maximizes mean array gain; for a Gaussian directional model, an equal-amplitude receiver is optimized by steering towards the conditional mean. Mean rate requires a different objective. We prove that the RSMA common-rate water level is jointly concave in the users' receive gains and derive a semidefinite relaxation with a computable global upper bound.
