abstract: ArXiv:2610.14524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a two-sided singular stochastic control problem in which changes in consumption carry utility costs and the risk premium follows the mean-reverting Kim-Omberg model. Optimal consumption is reflected between two moving barriers given by thresholds that depend on the current risk premium. These thresholds are the stopping boundaries of a Dynkin game for a two-dimensional diffusion driven by a single Brownian motion. A sharp occupation estimate shows that they are Lipschitz in logarithmic scale, uniformly in the cost of reducing consumption, and that smooth fit holds along the diffusion direction at every contact point. Outside a bounded interval of risk premia and at most two further points, the thresholds are infinitely differentiable. As the reduction cost grows, optimal consumption converges to the ratcheting policy.
tldr: The paper solves a two-sided singular stochastic control problem for optimal consumption adjustment under mean-reverting risk premia, characterizing moving thresholds via a Dynkin game.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how utility costs from changing consumption interact with a mean-reverting risk premium, extending consumption models with frictions.
method: They formulate the problem as a two-sided singular stochastic control problem and connect the optimal thresholds to the stopping boundaries of a Dynkin game for a two-dimensional diffusion driven by one Brownian motion.
result: The thresholds are shown to be Lipschitz in logarithmic scale and smooth-fit along the diffusion direction; outside a bounded interval of risk premia and at most two points, they are infinitely differentiable, and as reduction cost grows, optimal consumption converges to a ratcheting policy.
conclusion: The work provides a sharp mathematical characterization of consumption adjustment boundaries under mean-reverting risk premia, with implications for ratcheting behavior and regularity of optimal policies.

title: Argos: A Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture For Distributed Edge Security Orchestration
authors: Agustin Javier Di Bartolo, Mohammadhossein Homaei, Andres Caro, Mar Avila
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing adoption of distributed edge devices for security auditing and operational monitoring exposes limitations in lightweight control mechanisms traditionally used to manage such nodes. While commercial Command-and-Control (C2) platforms offer advanced orchestration features, their licensing constraints, operational complexity, and proprietary nature limit accessibility for small and medium-sized enterprises and research environments. This paper presents Argos, a multi-tenant SaaS C2 architecture designed for transparent, automated, and long-term orchestration of distributed edge devices. The framework implements a structured control plane with role-based access control (RBAC), tenant isolation, persistent task management, and cron-based workflow automation. Unlike operator-driven or stateless execution models, Argos enables scheduled and autonomous coordination of security tasks across heterogeneous environments. To formally substantiate its isolation guarantees, the platform is modeled through a set-theoretic authorization framework, and a tenant non-interference property is proven. The proposed architecture was evaluated across three geographically distributed edge devices, executing 810 automated tasks mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Results demonstrate a global failure rate of 3.33% (95% Wilson confidence interval: [2.30%, 4.81%]) with no statistically significant difference across ARM and x86 architectures ( 2 = 1.55, p = 0.21), and stable operation under heterogeneous latency conditions, including intercontinental deployments. To ensure scientific transparency and reproducibility, the evaluation methodology, sanitized datasets, and statistical scripts have been made publicly available in an open-source repository.
tldr: Argos is a multi-tenant SaaS command-and-control architecture for distributed edge security orchestration, with set-theoretic RBAC and proven tenant non-interference, evaluated on 810 automated MITRE ATT&CK tasks.
motivation: Commercial C2 platforms are too costly, complex, and proprietary for small-to-medium enterprises and research environments managing distributed edge devices for security auditing.
method: The paper designs a structured control plane with RBAC, tenant isolation, persistent task management, and cron-based workflow automation, models it via set-theoretic authorization, and proves a tenant non-interference property.
result: Evaluation across three geographically distributed edge devices executing 810 tasks yielded a global failure rate of 3.33% (95% Wilson CI [2.30%, 4.81%]) with no significant ARM/x86 difference (χ²=1.55, p=0.21).
conclusion: Argos provides transparent, automated, long-term orchestration for heterogeneous edge security tasks, with reproducibility supported by open-source datasets and scripts.

title: An Empirical Case Study Of Prompt Engineering Strategies For Bypassing Multi-Layer Agent Security Defenses
authors: Chengwei Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The OpenClaw Security Attack and Defense Challenge evaluates AI agent robustness through a three-stage defense pipeline: skill file scanning (Stage 1), instruction safety evaluation (Stage 2), and attack trajectory scoring (Stage 3). This paper presents an empirical case study of prompt engineering strategies against these layers across 19 attack targets in Enterprise OA, E-commerce, and Smart Home scenarios. I document both successful and failed strategies, with an emphasis on the observed trade-off between instruction safety (Stage 2) and attack execution accuracy (Stage 3). The final online score is 0.2630, with 5 of 19 tasks achieving full bypass. The results suggest that multi-layer defenses, reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints, substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.
tldr: An empirical case study of prompt engineering attacks against a three-stage AI-agent security defense pipeline, achieving full bypass on 5 of 19 tasks.
motivation: The OpenClaw Security Attack and Defense Challenge motivates a systematic study of how far prompt engineering alone can penetrate layered agent defenses in enterprise, e-commerce, and smart-home scenarios.
method: Manual prompt engineering strategies were applied against 19 attack targets and evaluated across three defense stages: skill file scanning, instruction safety evaluation, and attack trajectory scoring.
result: The final online score was 0.2630, with 5 of 19 tasks achieving full bypass; a trade-off was observed between satisfying instruction safety (Stage 2) and maintaining attack execution accuracy (Stage 3).
conclusion: Multi-layer defenses reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.

title: When The Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity For Deployment And Coding-Agent Approvals
authors: Md Imran Hossen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.15137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment tool's own record of its inputs or a manifest declared in the repository.
tldr: The paper defines authority-set integrity for binding approvals to every repository file that an authorized run reads, showing that ordinary edits outside the approved file can bypass deployment checks.
motivation: Approvals typically bind only the explicitly approved object, such as a workflow file or command, while the subsequent run depends on other mutable repository files that determine deployment behavior and policy outcomes.
method: The authors analyze 542 commits across 20 public repositories, demonstrate concrete policy-escalation edits on two repositories, and examine coding-agent attempts to produce sound authority-set bindings.
result: About 54.6% of commits that change files read by the run leave the approved file untouched, and edits outside the approved workflow can add a bucket-write policy or remove required human approval while passing checks on the approved file.
conclusion: A checker should not trust an agent-provided file set; it should compute the digest itself and derive the authority set from a verifiable source such as the deployment tool's input record or a repository manifest.

title: Exponential Quantum Advantage In Stationary Signal Sensing
authors: Changhun Oh Sojeong Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sensing time-varying signals is essential for precision measurement and for characterizing fluctuations in physical systems. In this work, we show that quantum entanglement provides an exponential advantage in the acquisition time required to learn the temporal statistics of a stationary classical signal. The task is to estimate the characteristic function of joint displacements on selected bosonic modes within a fixed-duration window, using continuous measurements of one signal realization. We present an entanglement-assisted scheme based on two-mode squeezed probes and local Bell measurements with protected idlers, and bound its acquisition time accounting for readout noise and correlations between signal windows. For a strictly stationary pulse family, it achieves polynomial acquisition time at inverse-polynomial accuracy with logarithmic squeezing and polynomial photon number. On the other hand, we prove that any local idler-free protocols require acquisition time exponential in the number of selected temporal modes per window. This lower bound holds for both sequentially prepared and arbitrarily temporally entangled probes, allowing non-Gaussian inputs and measurements and causal classical feedback, as long as each output is measured destructively within its time bin. These results establish an exponential quantum learning advantage for a single continuously monitored stationary signal, with the sensing cost measured by total acquisition time.

title: Watermarking For Byzantine Robust Llm Training
authors: Leixu Huang, Zedian Shao, Teodora Baluta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.14289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM watermarking has emerged as a promising approach for detecting downstream model misuse in centralized settings, but extending it to federated learning (FL) presents unique challenges. In particular, FL systems often rely on strong robust aggregators to defend against poisoning attacks. We empirically show that a malicious server can exploit these same aggregators as effective watermark-removal mechanisms during training, causing representative existing LLM watermarking methods to fail detection in the final model. To address this limitation, we formalize the problem as a constrained optimization task and propose CamoMark, an aggregator-agnostic watermarking scheme for embedding robust watermarks in FL. CamoMark optimizes watermarked updates to become inliers, maintaining bounded deviation from the distribution of clean updates, while preserving sufficient watermark signal for reliable detection. Evaluated on Qwen fine-tuned on the Alpaca dataset, CamoMark achieves a detection confidence of [MATH]-value [MATH] using only 3.3% watermarked data. The watermark also remains robust to a range of post-training removal attacks, including continued fine-tuning on clean data, pruning, and model distillation. At higher watermark ratios, detection confidence improves substantially, reaching [MATH]-value [MATH] at a 13.3% watermark ratio.
tldr: This paper proposes CamoMark, an aggregator-agnostic watermarking scheme for robust watermark embedding in federated learning of large language models, addressing watermark removal by Byzantine-robust aggregators.
motivation: LLM watermarking is useful for detecting model misuse in centralized settings, but federated learning systems often use robust aggregators that malicious servers can exploit to remove watermarks during training.
method: The authors formalize watermark embedding as a constrained optimization problem and design CamoMark to make watermarked updates appear as inliers while preserving detectable watermark signal.
result: Evaluated on Qwen fine-tuned on Alpaca, CamoMark achieves reliable detection using only 3.3% watermarked data and improves further at a 13.3% watermark ratio, while remaining robust to continued fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation.
conclusion: CamoMark provides a practical watermarking approach for federated LLM training that is resilient to robust aggregation and post-training removal attacks.
